questions.question: If a network round trip normally takes about 1 ms, what does an asynchronous packet network guarantee about the maximum delay?

options.text: No upper bound at all: a packet may be delayed arbitrarily long, or never arrive
A bound of roughly ten times the normal round trip, about 10 ms
A bound equal to TCP's retransmission timeout for the connection
A bound set by the size of the switch buffers along the path

questions.explanation: An asynchronous packet network (the internet, most datacenter Ethernet) tries to deliver packets as fast as it can but promises nothing about when, or whether, they arrive. The usual 1 ms says nothing about the worst case: queues at switches and receivers can grow without limit, a full buffer drops the packet, and retransmission adds further waiting. A retransmission timeout governs when TCP resends, not when delivery is guaranteed, and switch buffers bound one queue, not the whole path. Because there is no maximum delay, a timeout can never prove that a remote node is dead rather than slow.

questions.question: Which of these distributed-database topics are about handling faults and runtime edge cases, rather than about data formats changing over time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replica failover when a leader node becomes unavailable
Replication lag causing reads to return stale data
Concurrency control to stop transactions racing each other
Schema evolution keeping old and new encodings compatible

questions.explanation: Failover after a leader becomes unavailable, stale reads caused by replication lag, and concurrency control for racing transactions are all about coping with things going wrong while the system runs: nodes fail, data arrives late, and operations interleave badly. Schema evolution is different in kind: it deals with old and new code reading each other's encoded data, a compatibility problem that exists even when nothing fails.

optionExplanations.a: Leader unavailability forces a replicated system to detect the failure, choose a replacement and redirect traffic without creating two active leaders.
optionExplanations.b: Asynchronous propagation lets followers return older values, so applications need explicit guarantees such as read-after-write or monotonic reads.
optionExplanations.c: Concurrent transactions can invalidate one another's assumptions, requiring isolation mechanisms that prevent or detect harmful interleavings.
optionExplanations.d: Schema evolution concerns compatibility between old and new data encodings; it is a change-management problem that exists even when nothing fails at runtime.

questions.question: Properties of a distributed algorithm are often split into safety properties and liveness properties. How strictly must each kind hold?

options.text: Safety must hold in every situation the system model allows; liveness may come with caveats
Liveness must hold in every situation; safety only needs to hold eventually
Both must hold at every moment in every situation, with no caveats at all
Safety constrains performance; liveness constrains the integrity of data

questions.explanation: Safety informally means 'nothing bad happens' (for example, no two clients receive the same fencing token): if it is violated you can point to the moment it broke, and the damage cannot be undone, so algorithms require it to hold even if all nodes crash or the network fails. Liveness means 'something good eventually happens' (for example, a request eventually gets a response); it may be false at a given moment yet still be satisfied later, so it is allowed caveats such as 'only if a majority of nodes are up and the network eventually recovers'. Requiring liveness unconditionally is impossible: if every node crashes, nothing can respond.

questions.question: What fundamentally distinguishes writing software for a distributed system from writing it for a single computer?

options.text: Partial failure: some parts can fail while others keep working, unpredictably
Each operation on a healthy node becomes nondeterministic, unlike on one computer
All data must be serialized before it is shared, which is the main source of bugs
Faults can be detected only in production, because distributed code cannot be tested

questions.explanation: A single computer with working hardware is deterministic, and when its hardware fails it usually fails completely (kernel panic, failure to boot). A distributed system has independent parts connected by a network, so some parts can be broken while others are fine, and an operation that involves several nodes may sometimes succeed and sometimes fail unpredictably; because message delays are also nondeterministic, you may not even know whether it succeeded. Individual healthy nodes are still deterministic, serialization is a mechanical concern rather than the core difficulty, and distributed faults can and should be tested, for example by deliberately injecting them.

questions.question: If faults in a distributed system are inevitable, how is the engineer's task best defined?

options.text: To build systems that keep meeting their guarantees despite faults
To eliminate every possible fault from the system's design and hardware
To detect faults as quickly as possible and then stop the whole system
To document every failure mode, leaving their handling to the operators

questions.explanation: Faults cannot be eliminated from networks, clocks and machines, so the goal is fault tolerance: the system as a whole continues to do its job, meaning it meets the guarantees its users rely on, even while some components misbehave. Fast detection is useful but is only a first step, and stopping everything on a fault is the supercomputer approach, which is unacceptable for an online service. Documentation does not make a system keep working.

questions.question: Which three sources of uncertainty make it hard for a node in a distributed system to know what is really happening?

options.text: Unreliable networks, unreliable clocks, and unpredictable process pauses
Schema changes, evolving data encodings, and API versioning
Replication lag, uneven partition sizes, and slow queries
Compiler bugs, type errors, and memory leaks in the application

questions.explanation: A node learns about the rest of the system only through messages, which may be lost or arbitrarily delayed; it interprets those messages using a local clock that may be wrong or jump; and its own execution may be paused (for example by garbage collection) for an unknown time without it noticing. Together these mean a node can only guess at other nodes' state. Schema and encoding changes are compatibility issues, replication lag and skew are consequences or performance concerns, and ordinary program bugs exist on a single machine too.

questions.question: When a program on a single computer encounters a problem, how does the computer usually behave?

options.text: Predictably: either it works or it doesn't, rarely something in between
Unpredictably, because of variability in the underlying hardware
Predictably, but only while the machine is under light load
It always fails partially, exactly as a distributed system does

questions.explanation: With correct hardware, the same operation always produces the same result, so a single computer is deterministic; apparent flakiness is usually a software bug. When the hardware does develop a fault, computers are deliberately designed to fail completely rather than return wrong results. The result is that an individual computer is usually either fully functional or entirely broken, not something in between, which is exactly the property a distributed system loses.

questions.question: When a single computer develops a hardware problem, such as memory corruption or a loose connector, what is the usual consequence?

options.text: Total failure — a kernel panic, a blue screen, or a failure to boot
Partial degradation, in which wrong results are returned to callers
Silent data corruption that produces no visible symptom at all
Reduced throughput, while operation remains entirely correct

questions.explanation: Single computers are built so that an internal fault escalates into a total failure, such as a kernel panic, a 'blue screen of death', or a failure to start up, rather than letting the machine keep running and return incorrect results. Wrong results and silent corruption are what designers try to avoid, because they are harder to deal with than a crash. Total failure is easy to notice and reason about; partial degradation is not.

questions.question: Why are single computers deliberately designed to crash completely on an internal fault rather than keep running?

options.text: Because wrong results are more confusing to deal with than a crash
Because crashing is cheaper to implement than any kind of error recovery
Because a crash lets the hardware repair the fault automatically on reboot
Because operating systems are unable to detect any hardware faults at all

questions.explanation: If a computer kept running after an internal fault it might quietly return incorrect results, and wrong results are difficult and confusing to deal with. By failing completely, the computer preserves an idealized model in which every result it does produce is correct. A reboot may clear a software glitch but does not repair hardware, and operating systems can detect many faults; the choice is about keeping results trustworthy, not about cost.

questions.question: What does the idealized, deterministic model presented by a single computer hide from software?

options.text: Physical hardware faults, by crashing outright instead of returning wrong results
The network latency between the computer's components, by making it constant
Concurrency between threads, by running only one instruction stream at a time
Nothing: physical faults are exposed to programs as error codes they must handle

questions.explanation: Hardware is a physical device that can suffer bit flips, timing variation and broken connections, but a computer presents a model with mathematical perfection: a CPU instruction always does the same thing and data written to memory or disk stays intact. It maintains that illusion by escalating faults to a total crash. Threads still run concurrently and programs do not normally handle raw hardware errors. In a distributed system the illusion cannot be maintained across machines, so software must confront the messy physical reality directly.

questions.question: An experienced engineer listed failures seen in practice: long network partitions inside one datacenter, power-distribution-unit and switch failures, accidental power cycles of whole racks, whole-datacenter backbone and power failures, and a truck crashing into a datacenter's cooling system. What do such reports show? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Failures can be correlated, taking out a whole rack or datacenter at once
Network partitions can occur even within a single datacenter
Physical events unrelated to software, such as power or cooling loss, can stop healthy machines
Faults hit one machine at a time and independently, so copies on two adjacent racks are always enough

questions.explanation: The list shows that in the physical world a remarkably wide range of things go wrong: partitions inside one building, power and network gear failing, whole racks or datacenters going down together, and accidents with no connection to software. Because many of these take out groups of machines at once, faults are not independent, and placing replicas close together does not protect against them.

optionExplanations.a: Power cycles of whole racks and whole-datacenter backbone or power failures disable many machines simultaneously, so failures are correlated rather than independent.
optionExplanations.b: Long-lived network partitions within a single datacenter appear in the list, showing that a controlled local network can still split into parts that cannot communicate.
optionExplanations.c: A truck hitting the cooling system or a failed power-distribution unit can stop machines whose software and hardware are perfectly healthy.
optionExplanations.d: Rack-level and datacenter-level failures contradict the idea of independent single-machine faults; two adjacent racks can share power, switches or the building itself.

questions.question: In a distributed system, what is a partial failure, and what makes it hard to handle?

options.text: Some parts fail while others work, nondeterministically, so you may not know if an operation succeeded
Exactly half of the nodes are down at once, and the difficulty is the resulting loss of half the capacity
A write is only partly stored on disk, and the difficulty is repairing the torn record
Responses are slow but always arrive, and the difficulty is the extra latency for users

questions.explanation: A partial failure is when some components of a system are broken in some unpredictable way while others work fine. It is hard because it is nondeterministic: an operation involving several nodes and the network may sometimes work and sometimes fail, and because message delays are also unpredictable, the caller may not even learn whether it succeeded. It is not defined by any particular fraction of nodes, by torn writes, or by slowness alone; slowness that never ends in a response is indistinguishable from failure.

questions.question: Large-scale computing ranges from high-performance computing (HPC) to cloud computing. Which statements correctly characterize this spectrum? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: HPC uses supercomputers with thousands of CPUs for computationally intensive scientific tasks such as weather forecasting
Cloud computing is often associated with multi-tenant datacenters, commodity machines on IP networks, elastic allocation and metered billing
Traditional enterprise datacenters lie somewhere between HPC and cloud computing
Cloud computing is a precisely defined technical term with a single agreed industry meaning

questions.explanation: At one end, HPC runs computation-heavy scientific jobs on supercomputers; at the other, cloud computing serves many tenants on commodity machines over IP networks with on-demand resources and pay-per-use billing. Enterprise datacenters sit in between. Cloud computing is not well defined: it is a loose cluster of associated characteristics rather than a formal specification. These philosophies lead to very different ways of handling faults.

optionExplanations.a: HPC applies thousands of tightly coupled CPUs to scientific workloads such as weather forecasting or molecular dynamics, which can be stopped and restarted.
optionExplanations.b: Multi-tenancy, commodity nodes, Ethernet/IP networking, elastic allocation and metered billing are the characteristics commonly associated with cloud computing.
optionExplanations.c: Traditional enterprise datacenters are neither specialized supercomputers nor multi-tenant public clouds; they sit between those two extremes of the spectrum.
optionExplanations.d: Cloud computing has no single precise definition; it is a loose set of associated characteristics, so treating it as a strict specification is the misconception.

questions.question: How does a typical supercomputer (HPC) job deal with the failure of one node?

options.text: It checkpoints state periodically; on a failure, it stops and restarts from the last checkpoint
It routes the failed node's work to spare nodes automatically, so the job continues without interruption
It replicates all state continuously to other nodes, so no checkpoint is ever needed and work never stops
It ignores the failed node and continues, accepting degraded or partial results

questions.explanation: A supercomputer job periodically writes a checkpoint of its computation to durable storage. If a node fails, the usual response is to stop the entire workload, repair the node, and restart from the last checkpoint. The supercomputer therefore handles partial failure by escalating it to total failure, much like a single computer that crashes on a fault. That is acceptable for offline batch computation, but not for an online service that must keep answering users.

questions.question: Why can't an internet service handle faults the way a supercomputer batch job does?

options.text: An online service must keep serving users with low latency; a batch job can stop and restart with little impact
An internet service can stop for repair because users retry later; a batch job cannot be interrupted
Both must avoid downtime, so both rely on checkpointing and restarting the whole cluster
Neither can tolerate faults, so both depend on specialized, highly reliable hardware

questions.explanation: Many internet applications are online: users expect low-latency responses at any time, so stopping the whole cluster for repair is unacceptable. An offline batch job such as a weather simulation can be stopped and restarted from a checkpoint with fairly low impact. The availability requirement is therefore what rules out stop-and-repair for internet services and forces them to tolerate partial failure while continuing to run.

questions.question: How does the hardware of typical cloud services differ from that of supercomputers?

options.text: Clouds use commodity machines that fail more often; supercomputers use reliable specialized nodes and RDMA
Clouds use specialized, highly reliable nodes, while supercomputers use commodity machines connected by Ethernet
Both use the same commodity hardware and networks, differing only in their software
Cloud nodes communicate through shared memory and RDMA; supercomputer nodes communicate only over the internet

questions.explanation: Supercomputers are typically built from specialized hardware in which each node is quite reliable, and nodes communicate through shared memory and remote direct memory access (RDMA). Cloud services use commodity machines, which give equivalent performance at lower cost thanks to economies of scale but fail more often, connected by ordinary IP/Ethernet networks. Higher failure rates on cheaper parts are one reason cloud software must tolerate faults rather than avoid them.

questions.question: Why do supercomputers often use specialized network topologies such as multi-dimensional meshes and toruses?

options.text: Their HPC workloads have known communication patterns, which these topologies serve better
Ethernet cannot connect more than a few hundred nodes in one network
Clos topologies cannot provide high bisection bandwidth for large clusters
Specialized topologies remove the need to checkpoint the computation

questions.explanation: HPC jobs often have predictable communication patterns, so a purpose-built mesh or torus can yield better performance for exactly those exchanges. Large datacenter networks, by contrast, are usually IP and Ethernet arranged in Clos topologies, which provide high bisection bandwidth for varied, unpredictable traffic. Ethernet scales to very large datacenters, and the network topology has nothing to do with whether a job needs checkpoints.

questions.question: In a system with thousands of nodes, why does 'stop everything and restart' become an impractical way to handle faults?

options.text: Something is nearly always broken, so it would spend much of its time recovering
Scale lowers the chance that anything is broken, so restarts become unnecessary
Scale does not change how often something is broken, only how long restarts take
Scale makes restarting everything cheaper than repairing an individual node

questions.explanation: The more components a system has, the more likely it is that at least one is broken at any moment; with thousands of nodes it is reasonable to assume something is always broken. If the only error-handling strategy is to give up and restart, a large system ends up spending a lot of its time recovering from faults instead of doing useful work. Redundancy can help tolerate faults but does not reduce how often some component fails.

questions.question: If a distributed system can tolerate failed nodes and keep working as a whole, what operational benefits follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A rolling upgrade: restarting one node at a time while the service keeps serving users
In the cloud, killing a poorly performing virtual machine and requesting a new one
Upgrading every node simultaneously without any interruption to the service
No longer needing durable storage or backups, since a failed node's state can never be lost

questions.explanation: Tolerating failed nodes means the loss of any one node, whether accidental or deliberate, does not stop the service. That allows operators to restart nodes one at a time for upgrades and to replace an underperforming virtual machine on demand. It does not make the whole cluster expendable at once, and it does not make data indestructible: tolerating a node failure depends on durable state elsewhere.

optionExplanations.a: Because the rest of the cluster keeps serving while one node is down, operators can restart and upgrade nodes one at a time without a user-visible outage.
optionExplanations.b: Treating virtual machines as replaceable lets operators discard a slow instance and provision another, hoping it is faster, while other nodes carry the load.
optionExplanations.c: Tolerating some failed nodes does not mean tolerating all nodes down at once; restarting every node simultaneously would take the service offline.
optionExplanations.d: Node fault tolerance relies on replicated or durable state; it does not make state impossible to lose, so durability and backups remain necessary.

questions.question: Compared with a supercomputer whose nodes sit close together, why does a geographically distributed deployment face harsher network conditions?

options.text: Its traffic most likely crosses the internet, which is slower and less reliable than a local network
Clock synchronization between nodes becomes impossible once they are in different regions
Replication protocols are unable to operate between distant regions at all
Geographic deployments require dedicated circuit-switched links between regions

questions.explanation: Keeping data geographically close to users reduces their access latency, but nodes in different regions then usually communicate over the internet, which is slow and unreliable compared with a local network. Supercomputers generally assume all their nodes are physically close. Clocks can be synchronized across regions (imperfectly), replication across regions is common, and inter-region links are normally packet-switched.

questions.question: To make distributed systems work, what must their software accept and build in?

options.text: The possibility of partial failure, with fault-tolerance mechanisms in software
Nothing special, provided the hardware is good enough to prevent partial failure
Total failure on any fault, restarting from a checkpoint as a supercomputer does
Perfect reliability, which software can guarantee once it is correctly designed

questions.explanation: Partial failure cannot be engineered away with better hardware, and stop-and-restart is unacceptable for online services, so distributed software must expect some components to fail and include mechanisms to tolerate it: building a reliable system from unreliable components. Even then there is no perfect reliability, so designers need to understand the limits of what can realistically be promised.

questions.question: Why should even a small distributed system of only a few nodes plan for partial failure? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Unlikely faults do happen, so it is worth deliberately creating them in testing to see what happens
Even if most components usually work, sooner or later some part will fail, so fault handling belongs in the design
Operators need to know what behavior to expect from the software when a fault occurs
It is reasonable to assume faults are rare in a small system and simply hope for the best

questions.explanation: In a small system most components work most of the time, but over a long enough period some part will fail, and the software must handle it somehow. That handling should be designed and tested, including fairly unlikely faults that are artificially injected, and operators should know what the software will do. In distributed systems, suspicion, pessimism and paranoia pay off; hoping faults stay rare leaves recovery paths untested.

optionExplanations.a: Fault injection exposes how the system really behaves under rare but plausible faults, which ordinary happy-path testing rarely reaches.
optionExplanations.b: Over a system's lifetime even a few components eventually crash, pause or lose connectivity, so partial-failure behavior must be part of the design.
optionExplanations.c: Operators need a predictable response to faults so they can tell safe degradation apart from corruption or a stuck cluster and act accordingly.
optionExplanations.d: Rarity is not protection over a long lifetime; hoping for the best leaves untested recovery paths that fail unpredictably when the fault finally occurs.

questions.question: Intuitively, one might say a system can be only as reliable as its least reliable component. Why is that intuition wrong for computer systems?

options.text: Higher layers can build a more reliable system from less reliable parts, as TCP does over IP
Adding redundancy always makes the overall system perfectly reliable
Component reliability stops mattering once the software is well tested
It is not wrong: no layer can ever be more reliable than the layer beneath it

questions.explanation: It is an old idea in computing to construct a more reliable system from a less reliable base. Error-correcting codes transmit data accurately over a channel that flips bits, and TCP provides retransmission, deduplication and ordering on top of IP, which may drop, delay, duplicate or reorder packets. The improvement has limits, though: such a layer cannot make the system perfect, and the parts underneath still matter.

questions.question: Error-correcting codes and TCP both build a more reliable layer on an unreliable one. Which statements about what they achieve and where they stop are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Error-correcting codes let data cross a channel that occasionally flips bits, such as a noisy wireless link
TCP turns IP's possible drops, duplicates and reordering into retransmitted, deduplicated, in-order delivery
Error correction handles a few bit errors, but a channel swamped by interference has a fundamental capacity limit
TCP's retransmission hides packet loss and also removes variable network delay

questions.explanation: Both techniques mask some low-level faults, but not all. IP may drop, delay, duplicate or reorder packets; TCP fixes loss, duplication and reordering but cannot remove delay, and retransmission itself adds delay. Error-correcting codes fix a limited number of bit errors, and beyond that there is a fundamental limit on how much data a noisy channel can carry. The delay that TCP cannot hide is the root of the unreliable-network problems in distributed systems.

optionExplanations.a: Error-correcting codes add redundancy so a receiver can reconstruct data after a limited number of bit errors, masking a noisy physical channel.
optionExplanations.b: TCP retransmits missing packets, removes duplicates and reassembles packets in the order sent, giving applications a more reliable stream than raw IP.
optionExplanations.c: Redundancy has a finite correction capacity; interference severe enough to exceed the channel's information limit cannot be repaired.
optionExplanations.d: Retransmission makes delivery take longer and network queues stay variable, so TCP improves reliability without removing or bounding delay.

questions.question: TCP hides packet loss but not network delay, and error-correcting codes fail under heavy interference. If such a higher-level layer is not perfectly reliable, why is it still worth having?

options.text: It handles tricky low-level faults, so the rest are easier to reason about
With enough redundancy added, the layer can eventually be made perfectly reliable
It removes the need for any error handling in the application above it
It guarantees an upper bound on latency in exchange for occasionally losing data

questions.explanation: A more reliable layer is useful even though it is imperfect, because it takes care of some of the fiddly low-level faults (lost, duplicated or reordered packets; flipped bits) and leaves a smaller set of faults that are usually easier to reason about and deal with. It cannot be made perfect, applications still need to handle what leaks through (for example, timeouts), and it gives no latency bound.

questions.question: What is a shared-nothing architecture for a distributed system?

options.text: Machines with their own memory and disk, communicating only over a network
Machines that all access one shared disk array but keep separate memory
Machines that read each other's memory directly using remote direct memory access
Machines that each run a different software implementation so they share no bugs

questions.explanation: In a shared-nothing system each machine has its own memory and disk, and one machine cannot access another's memory or disk except by sending requests over the network, which is the only communication channel. It has become the dominant approach for internet services because it needs no special hardware, can use commodity cloud services, and can achieve high reliability through redundancy across geographically distributed datacenters. The price is that every interaction goes over an unreliable network.

questions.question: What is an asynchronous packet network, such as the internet or most datacenter Ethernet?

options.text: A network that guarantees neither when nor whether a packet arrives
A network with bounded delay that guarantees every message is delivered
A network that always delivers messages in the order they were sent
A circuit-switched network with bandwidth reserved for each connection

questions.explanation: In an asynchronous packet network one node can send a packet to another, but the network guarantees neither delivery nor a time by which it will arrive. A sender therefore cannot distinguish a lost message from one that is merely delayed, or from a slow or crashed recipient. Ordering is not guaranteed either (TCP adds it), and circuit-switched networks with reserved bandwidth are the contrasting, synchronous design.

questions.question: You send a request over an asynchronous network and receive no response. Which explanations are consistent with that silence? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The request was lost, or is still waiting in a queue and will be delivered later
The remote node crashed, or is temporarily paused, for example by garbage collection
The remote node rejected the request with an error message that reached you
The remote node processed the request, but its response was lost or delayed

questions.explanation: When no response arrives, any of several things may have happened: the request was lost or delayed; the remote node crashed or paused; or the node processed the request but the response was lost or delayed. These cases are indistinguishable to the sender, who knows only that nothing has arrived yet. A delivered error message is a response, so it is not an explanation of silence.

optionExplanations.a: A request can disappear before arrival or sit in an overloaded queue, and both look identical to the sender: no response yet.
optionExplanations.b: A crashed node and a healthy node stuck in a long pause both stay silent, and the sender cannot tell them apart until communication resumes.
optionExplanations.c: An error message that reaches the sender is itself a response, so this case does not produce silence and is not consistent with the situation described.
optionExplanations.d: The node may have completed the operation while its reply was lost or delayed, which is why a blind retry can repeat the operation.

questions.question: Why is a missing response from a remote node ambiguous?

options.text: Because a lost request, a crashed or paused node, and a lost reply all produce the same silence
Because packet networks have no way to acknowledge that a packet arrived
Because the sender's clock may have recorded the wrong time of sending
It is not ambiguous: a TCP acknowledgment shows the application handled the request

questions.explanation: A sender observes only the absence of a reply, and that is compatible with the request being lost or delayed, the receiver having failed or paused, or the reply being lost or delayed. The only way to learn whether a packet was delivered is for the recipient to respond, and that response can itself be lost. TCP acknowledgments exist but show only that the remote operating system received the bytes; the application may crash before acting on them. Clock errors are irrelevant to this ambiguity.

questions.question: What does a timeout tell you, and what residual uncertainty remains?

options.text: You stop waiting, still unsure whether the request arrived
It tells you definitively that the remote node has died
It tells you the request was definitely not processed
It tells you the response was lost rather than the request

questions.explanation: When a timeout expires, the caller has decided to stop waiting; it has learned nothing about what happened remotely. The request may have been lost, may still be queued and delivered later, or may have been processed with the reply lost or delayed. So a timeout proves neither that the node is dead nor that the request was not processed, which is why a retry after a timeout can perform an operation twice.

questions.question: One study of a medium-sized datacenter measured how often network faults occur. What did it find?

options.text: About 12 network faults per month, half disconnecting one machine and half a whole rack
About 2 network faults per year, all of them disconnecting a whole rack
About 100 network faults per month, all of them disconnecting one machine
About one network fault per year, disconnecting a single machine

questions.explanation: The study found roughly 12 network faults per month, about 144 a year, with half disconnecting a single machine and half disconnecting an entire rack. The point is that network problems are surprisingly common even in a controlled datacenter run by one company, and that some faults cut off many machines at once, so software must be designed to handle them.

questions.question: A study of failures in datacenter networking gear (top-of-rack switches, aggregation switches, load balancers) looked at adding redundant equipment. Why did redundancy reduce faults less than hoped?

options.text: It does not guard against human error, such as misconfigured switches, a major cause of outages
Redundant gear adds more components that can break, so the total number of faults rises
Redundant switches cannot be used together on an Ethernet network
Most network outages come from applications, not from the network itself

questions.explanation: Redundant switches and links help when a single device or cable fails, but a human error such as a misconfiguration can affect every redundant path at once, and human error is a major cause of outages. Redundancy therefore does not reduce faults as much as you might hope. The study did not find that redundancy made things worse, and redundant gear is routinely used on Ethernet.

questions.question: As of the mid-2010s, how did public cloud networks compare with well-managed private datacenter networks?

options.text: Public clouds such as EC2 were notorious for transient glitches; private ones could be stabler
Well-managed private datacenter networks had faults too rare to be worth designing software for
Public clouds tended to be more stable than private datacenter networks, thanks to their scale
The two were equally unreliable, with no measurable difference between them

questions.explanation: At the time of writing, public cloud services such as EC2 were notorious for frequent transient network glitches, and a well-managed private datacenter network could be a stabler environment. Still, nobody is immune: a switch software upgrade can trigger a topology reconfiguration that delays packets for over a minute, sharks have damaged undersea cables, and interfaces can fail in strange ways. Whatever the environment, software must be prepared for network faults.

questions.question: A network interface was observed to drop all inbound packets while still sending outbound packets successfully. What does this show?

options.text: A link that works one way is not guaranteed to work the other way
Packet loss is always symmetric, so checking one direction is enough
The affected node will always detect such a fault itself immediately
TCP retransmission recovers from any fault in a network interface

questions.explanation: Network faults can be asymmetric: traffic may flow one way but not the other. A node with such a fault can keep sending while being deaf to replies (or vice versa), so a one-direction check can make a broken link look healthy and the node may not realize anything is wrong. Retransmission cannot help when every packet in one direction is dropped. Asymmetric faults are why nodes can be declared dead while believing themselves healthy.

questions.question: When one part of a network is cut off from the rest, why might you prefer the general term 'network fault' to 'network partition'?

options.text: To avoid confusion with partitions (shards) of a storage system
Because 'network partition' implies the fault is permanent
Because a network partition can occur only between datacenters
Because 'network fault' refers only to faults inside one machine

questions.explanation: A part of the network being cut off is often called a network partition or netsplit. In data systems, 'partition' also means a shard: a deliberate subset of the data stored on some nodes. Using 'network fault' avoids mixing up the two meanings. Partitions need not be permanent, can occur within a single datacenter, and 'network fault' covers any fault in the network between machines.

questions.question: What can happen when software meets a network fault whose handling was never defined or tested? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The cluster can deadlock and stay unable to serve requests even after the network recovers
The software can delete all of its data
It is guaranteed to fail safe, rejecting requests until an operator intervenes
It behaves exactly as it does on a healthy network, because TCP masks the fault

questions.explanation: If software is put in a situation its designers never anticipated, it may do arbitrary unexpected things. Real systems have become permanently deadlocked after a network fault even once the network healed, and failover analyses have found scenarios that delete data. There is no guarantee of safe behavior, and TCP cannot hide a fault that blocks communication. This is why network fault handling should be defined and deliberately tested.

optionExplanations.a: An untested state transition can leave nodes waiting on one another after connectivity returns, turning a temporary fault into a permanent outage.
optionExplanations.b: A badly designed failover or split-brain recovery can make destructive decisions; real analyses have found network-fault scenarios that lose all data.
optionExplanations.c: Fail-safe behavior must be designed and tested; untested handling is arbitrary, so there is no guarantee it will merely reject requests.
optionExplanations.d: TCP masks loss of individual packets but cannot make a cut-off network deliver anything, so the software's behavior does change during a fault.

questions.question: What distinguishes tolerating a network fault from merely handling it?

options.text: Tolerating keeps serving through the fault; handling may just show an error, then recover
They are the same thing, described with two different names
Tolerating means showing users an error message; handling means continuing to serve every request normally
Handling is unnecessary whenever the network is normally reliable, since rare faults can simply be ignored

questions.explanation: Handling network faults does not necessarily mean tolerating them: if your network is normally fairly reliable, a valid approach may be to show users an error message while the network has problems. What you must do is know how the software reacts to network problems and make sure the system recovers afterwards. Tolerance is the stronger goal of continuing to provide useful service during the fault. Even a reliable network has faults, so some handling is always necessary.

questions.question: Why is automatic detection of faulty nodes needed? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A load balancer must stop sending requests to a dead node, taking it out of rotation
With single-leader replication, a follower must be promoted to leader when the current leader fails
After every failover, the whole replication log must be recomputed from scratch on all nodes
Every node's clock must be kept synchronized, and failure detection is what performs that

questions.explanation: Many systems must decide automatically whether a node is dead. A load balancer has to stop sending requests to a dead node (take it out of rotation), and in single-leader replication a failed leader must be replaced by promoting a follower. Detection is hard because an unreliable network cannot reveal whether a silent node is dead, partitioned, delayed or paused. Failure detection does not rebuild replication logs or synchronize clocks; those are separate mechanisms.

optionExplanations.a: A load balancer must remove an unavailable endpoint or it will continue sending user requests into repeated timeouts and failures.
optionExplanations.b: Single-leader availability depends on noticing leader loss and promoting a follower so the system regains a write authority.
optionExplanations.c: Failover normally continues from replicated state and log positions; recomputing the entire replication log is neither the purpose of failure detection nor required.
optionExplanations.d: Clock synchronization estimates time offsets and is a separate protocol; determining node liveness does not synchronize every machine's clock.

questions.question: If you can reach a machine but no process is listening on the destination port (because it crashed), its operating system replies with a TCP RST or FIN. What does that reply tell you?

options.text: That nothing is accepting connections there, not how much of an earlier request was processed
That the earlier request was fully processed and committed before the process crashed and closed the port
That the earlier request was never processed, since the process died before reading it, so retrying is safe
That the whole machine has been powered down and is unreachable

questions.explanation: An RST or FIN gives fast, explicit feedback that the process is no longer accepting connections, which is better than waiting for a timeout. But if the process crashed while handling your request, you have no way of knowing how much of that request was actually carried out. The reply comes from a running operating system, so the machine itself is up. Retrying safely still requires idempotent operations or deduplication.

questions.question: You can query switch management interfaces to detect link failures. When is that option ruled out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you're connecting via the internet
If you're in a shared datacenter with no access to the switches themselves
If you can't reach the management interface due to a network problem
If the remote machine is powered down, since a powered-down machine cannot be distinguished from a healthy one

questions.explanation: Switch telemetry is useful only when you control and can reach the relevant management plane. Internet paths, shared facilities, or a fault blocking that interface remove the signal. Even available link data cannot establish how far an application request progressed.

optionExplanations.a: An application using the public internet cannot query and correlate management data from every independently operated switch along the route.
optionExplanations.b: A tenant in a shared facility normally lacks administrative access to provider switches, so link telemetry cannot be its failure oracle.
optionExplanations.c: The same network fault being diagnosed may block access to the management interface, removing the supposedly independent source of evidence.
optionExplanations.d: A powered-down host may cause a switch port status change that management can report; it does not itself prevent querying the switch interface.

questions.question: When a router is sure that the IP address you are trying to reach is unreachable, what may it send you, and how far can you trust it?

options.text: An ICMP Destination Unreachable packet, though routers cannot detect failures reliably either
A TCP RST on behalf of the destination host, proving that the host has crashed
An ICMP echo reply, which confirms that the destination host is down
Nothing at all, because routers have no way to report unreachable addresses

questions.explanation: A router may reply with ICMP Destination Unreachable, which is useful rapid feedback. However, the router has no magic failure detection: it is subject to the same limits as other participants in the network, and its message may itself be lost or delayed. Such feedback is helpful when it arrives but cannot be counted on, and it says nothing about whether the remote application processed an earlier request.

questions.question: What counts as reliable evidence that a request to a remote service actually succeeded?

options.text: A positive response from the application itself
A TCP acknowledgment from the remote host is sufficient
The absence of an error response is sufficient evidence
A timeout that has not yet expired is sufficient evidence

questions.explanation: Even if TCP acknowledges that a packet was delivered, that only means the remote operating system received the bytes; the application may crash before handling them. The absence of an error proves nothing, because errors can be lost too, and a timeout that has not yet expired just means you are still waiting. Only a positive response from the application itself shows the request was processed.

questions.question: When choosing the timeout for declaring a remote node dead, what is the fundamental trade-off?

options.text: Faster failure detection versus more risk of declaring a slow node dead
Throughput of the monitoring node versus the disk space used by its logs
Clock accuracy on each node versus the network bandwidth consumed
None: there is a standard correct value, such as 30 seconds, for all systems

questions.explanation: A long timeout means waiting a long time before a dead node is declared dead, during which users may wait or see errors. A short timeout detects faults faster but more often mistakes a temporary slowdown (a load spike on the node or network) for failure. Because network delays are unbounded and vary between environments, there is no universally correct value; it must be chosen experimentally for each system.

questions.question: Why is prematurely declaring a node dead problematic?

options.text: Because the node may be alive and midway through an action
Because the node's data will be deleted when it is declared dead
Because the node will not be able to rejoin the cluster afterwards
Because the clocks on the two nodes will drift further apart

questions.explanation: If the node is actually alive and in the middle of an action, such as sending an email, and another node takes over its responsibilities, the action may end up being performed twice. The 'dead' node also does not stop just because others have declared it dead, so two nodes may act at once. Declaring a node dead does not delete its data, and it may rejoin later; the danger is duplicated or conflicting work, plus the extra load the takeover places on other nodes.

questions.question: How can declaring nodes dead too quickly cause a cascading failure in a heavily loaded system?

options.text: Its load moves to other nodes, which overload and get declared dead too
It cannot: declaring nodes dead early sheds work and so reduces the total load
It affects only the node declared dead, so failures cannot spread to other nodes
Cascading failures come only from timeouts that are too long, never too short

questions.explanation: When a node is declared dead, its responsibilities move to other nodes, adding load to them and to the network. If the 'dead' node was actually just slow because the system was overloaded, moving its work makes the remaining nodes slower still, so they too start missing timeouts and being declared dead. In the extreme, all nodes declare each other dead and everything stops working. The work does not disappear; it is redistributed.

questions.question: Imagine a network where every packet is either delivered within time d or lost, and every non-failed node handles a request within time r. What is the longest a successful request can take to get a response, and what is it for d = 20 ms and r = 100 ms?

options.text: 2d + r, which is 140 ms
d + r, which is 120 ms
2(d + r), which is 240 ms
d + 2r, which is 220 ms

questions.explanation: The request travels to the node in at most d, the node processes it in at most r, and the response travels back in at most d, for a total of 2d + r. With d = 20 ms and r = 100 ms that is 20 + 100 + 20 = 140 ms. In such a system, no response after 140 ms would prove that the network or the remote node had failed, so 2d + r would be a reasonable timeout. Real asynchronous networks and servers give neither guarantee.

questions.question: Why is 2d + r not a safe hard timeout in ordinary distributed systems?

options.text: Neither network delay nor process time has a hard upper bound
Only the network assumption fails; response times are bounded
Only the response-time assumption fails; networks are bounded
Both assumptions hold in practice, which is why 2d + r is the standard timeout

questions.explanation: Networks and processes are usually fast, but neither packet delay nor process pause has a guaranteed maximum. A probabilistic observation cannot justify the hard 2d + r bound.

questions.question: Like travel times on roads, delays on computer networks vary. What is the most common cause of that variability?

options.text: Queueing, in switches, receiving hosts, hypervisors and TCP senders
Routing changes, which constantly alter the physical distance packets travel
Signal propagation speed, which varies with the temperature of the cable
Packet size, since larger packets always take proportionally longer to arrive

questions.explanation: Just as road travel times vary most because of traffic congestion, packet delays vary mostly because of queueing. Packets wait when several senders target the same switch output, when all CPU cores on the destination are busy, when a hypervisor buffers data for a paused virtual machine, and when TCP flow control holds data at the sender. Propagation distance and packet size are comparatively stable, so the unpredictable part of latency is the waiting.

questions.question: Where does queueing arise in a packet network? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At a switch, when several senders target the same outgoing link
At the destination, when all CPU cores are busy and the application is not ready
At a hypervisor, while the destination virtual machine is paused
In the cable itself, where signals travel more slowly while a link is busy

questions.explanation: Packets queue at switches whose output links are oversubscribed (and are dropped if the queue fills), in the destination operating system when no CPU core can take them, and in the virtual machine monitor while a VM is paused. TCP flow control (congestion avoidance or backpressure) adds a further queue at the sender before data even enters the network. The cable itself does not slow down under load: signal propagation speed is fixed, and the waiting happens in buffers.

optionExplanations.a: When several inputs target one outgoing link, the switch serializes those packets in a buffer and may drop them if that queue fills.
optionExplanations.b: After arrival, packets wait in operating-system buffers when all CPU cores are busy and the application cannot consume them yet.
optionExplanations.c: A paused virtual machine cannot drain incoming data, so the hypervisor or virtual network layer buffers it until that VM is scheduled.
optionExplanations.d: Signal propagation speed in copper or fiber is fixed by physics and does not depend on load; when a link is busy, packets wait in buffers at switches and hosts, not in the wire.

questions.question: When TCP loses a packet and recovers it, what delay does the application experience even though it never sees the loss?

options.text: Waiting for TCP's retransmission timeout, then for the resent packet
No delay, because TCP retransmits instantly as soon as a packet is sent
None from TCP: it never retransmits, leaving the application to handle loss
The application sees the loss itself, but no extra delay from recovering it

questions.explanation: TCP considers a packet lost if it is not acknowledged within a timeout calculated from observed round-trip times, and then retransmits it automatically. The application does not see the loss or the retransmission, but it does see the result: a delay made up of waiting for that timeout to expire and then waiting for the retransmitted packet to be acknowledged. Reliability is bought with extra, variable latency.

questions.question: Why do latency-sensitive applications such as videoconferencing and Voice over IP often use UDP rather than TCP?

options.text: Late data is worthless to them, and UDP skips flow control and retransmission
UDP eliminates every source of variable delay, including switch queues
UDP performs flow control but skips retransmission, so it is still fully reliable for these applications
UDP is more reliable than TCP, so fewer packets are lost overall

questions.explanation: Choosing between TCP and UDP is a trade-off between reliability and variability of delay. UDP does not perform flow control and does not retransmit lost packets, so it avoids some causes of variable delay, though packets can still wait in switch queues and behind CPU scheduling. For live audio or video, data that arrives too late is useless anyway, so giving up reliability costs little. UDP is not more reliable than TCP; it is simply less delayed.

questions.question: Why is retransmission pointless in a VoIP call?

options.text: Because resent audio would arrive after it was due to be played
Because UDP forbids retransmission at the protocol level
Because audio packets are too large to be retransmitted
Because voice data is not sensitive to errors in the first place

questions.explanation: In a live call, a lost packet's audio is due to be played almost immediately, and there is probably not enough time to retransmit it first; a resent packet would arrive too late to be useful. The application instead fills the missing time slot with silence and moves on, and any retry happens at the human level ('could you repeat that?'). UDP does not forbid an application from resending data, and the issue is timing, not packet size or the audio's sensitivity to errors.

questions.question: Why do network queueing delays grow especially large when a system is close to its maximum capacity?

options.text: With little spare capacity, queues fill faster than they drain
Packets travel physically farther across a network that is busy
TCP switches off its flow control when the network is near capacity
CPU scheduling becomes strictly deterministic when machines are busy

questions.explanation: A system with plenty of spare capacity can easily drain its queues, so bursts pass quickly. In a highly utilized system there is little slack to absorb a burst, so queues grow very quickly and take a long time to drain; queueing delay therefore has an especially wide range near saturation. Distance does not change with load, and TCP flow control and CPU scheduling keep operating; they are sources of variable delay, not cures for it.

questions.question: In public clouds and multi-tenant datacenters, what is a 'noisy neighbor'?

options.text: Another customer whose heavy use of shared links or CPUs makes your network delays unpredictable
A node that floods the cluster with heartbeat messages in order to detect failures faster than its peers
A virtual machine whose clock drifts faster than its host's, so its timestamps disturb other tenants' VMs
A replica that rejects writes because its local disk has filled up

questions.explanation: In multi-tenant environments, network links, switches, and even each machine's network interface and CPUs (when running in virtual machines) are shared among many customers. A batch workload such as MapReduce can easily saturate network links. Because you have no control over or insight into other customers' usage, someone nearby using a lot of resources can make your network delays highly variable.

questions.question: In an environment with unpredictable network delays, how should you choose a failure-detection timeout?

options.text: Measure round-trip times over time and derive the timeout from them
Use the maximum round-trip time observed on a single machine
Use whatever default value the database vendor recommends
Use the median of a one-minute sample of round-trip times

questions.explanation: There is no universally correct value, so timeouts must be chosen experimentally: measure the distribution of network round-trip times over an extended period and across many machines to learn how variable delays are, then weigh your application's needs to pick a trade-off between failure-detection delay and the risk of premature timeouts. A single machine, a one-minute sample or a median all underestimate the tail, and a vendor default knows nothing about your environment.

questions.question: Rather than using a configured constant timeout, what can a failure detector do to cope with changing network conditions?

options.text: Continually measure response times and jitter, and adjust the timeout, as Phi Accrual detectors do
Fix the timeout at the smallest round-trip time ever observed on the network, so failures are caught early
Never time out, and wait indefinitely for each response to arrive
Pick a random timeout for each request from a fixed range, so that false suspicions average out over time

questions.explanation: Systems can continually measure response times and their variability (jitter) and automatically adjust timeouts to the observed response-time distribution. A Phi Accrual failure detector does this, and it is used for example in Akka and Cassandra; TCP retransmission timeouts work similarly. The smallest observed round-trip time would cause constant false suspicion, waiting forever never detects a failure, and random timeouts ignore the actual delay distribution.

questions.question: Which network shows that bounded delays are achievable in principle, raising the question of why datacenter networks don't provide them?

options.text: The fixed-line telephone network, which reserves a circuit per call
The public internet, which reserves bandwidth for each TCP connection
Wi-Fi networks, which avoid congestion by transmitting over radio
Ethernet LANs, which are designed never to drop or delay packets

questions.explanation: The fixed-line (non-cellular, non-VoIP) telephone network is extremely reliable: delayed audio frames and dropped calls are rare. When a call is set up, the network establishes a circuit with a fixed, guaranteed amount of bandwidth along the entire route, so there is no queueing and the maximum latency is fixed. The internet and Ethernet are packet-switched and reserve nothing, and Wi-Fi suffers its own interference and contention.

questions.question: An ISDN telephone network runs at 4,000 frames per second, and each call is allocated 16 bits in every frame, in each direction. What does each side of the call get?

options.text: 64 kbit/s: 16 bits every 250 microseconds
32 kbit/s: 8 bits every 250 microseconds
16 kbit/s: 16 bits every millisecond
4 kbit/s: 1 bit every 250 microseconds

questions.explanation: 4,000 frames per second means one frame every 1/4,000 s = 250 microseconds. Each frame carries 16 bits for the call in each direction, so each side may send exactly 16 bits every 250 microseconds, which is 4,000 x 16 = 64,000 bits per second. Because that space is reserved in every frame at every hop, the call never queues behind other traffic and has a fixed maximum latency.

questions.question: Why does a circuit give bounded delay?

options.text: Because reserved space at each hop removes queueing
Because circuit routers are faster than packet routers
Because the circuit uses UDP in place of TCP framing
Because the volume of audio data is small enough to fit

questions.explanation: A circuit reserves bandwidth along every hop before communication begins. Competing traffic cannot consume that allocation, so data need not wait for capacity on the reserved path.

questions.question: Contrast a telephone circuit with a TCP connection.

options.text: A circuit reserves bandwidth for its call; TCP uses whatever is available
Both reserve bandwidth; a TCP connection simply reserves less of it
Each is opportunistic, and the circuit merely receives scheduling priority
A TCP connection reserves its bandwidth even while sitting idle

questions.explanation: Circuit switching reserves a fixed slice of capacity for the call. Packet switching shares capacity opportunistically among active senders, improving utilization at the cost of queueing.

questions.question: Why can't Ethernet and IP promise a maximum round-trip time?

options.text: Because packet-switched queues make delay unbounded
Because Ethernet is too slow to carry reserved circuits
Because the IP protocol is stateless between packets
Because IP addresses change too often to reserve a fixed path

questions.explanation: Without an end-to-end reservation, packets compete for each link and may queue behind bursts. Since queue length and retransmission behavior lack a hard bound, latency lacks one too.

questions.question: InfiniBand implements end-to-end flow control at the link layer. What does that achieve?

options.text: It reduces queueing in the network, though link congestion can still cause delays
It turns the network into a circuit-switched one, with fixed bandwidth reserved along every route
It eliminates all network delays, giving a hard upper bound on latency
It disables retransmission, so late packets are dropped as with UDP

questions.explanation: InfiniBand has some similarities to hybrid networks that support both circuit and packet switching: its link-layer flow control holds back senders before buffers overflow, which reduces queueing inside the network. Traffic still competes for finite links, though, so it can suffer delays from link congestion. It is not a circuit-switched network and does not give a hard latency bound.

questions.question: How can a packet-switched network emulate circuit switching, or provide statistically bounded delay?

options.text: Quality of service (packet prioritization and scheduling) plus admission control (rate-limiting senders)
By disabling TCP flow control so that every packet is sent immediately without waiting for acknowledgments
By assigning each flow its own reserved IP address range
By routing every flow over the shortest physical path, so that its packets never wait behind others

questions.explanation: Quality of service lets the network prioritize and schedule packets, and admission control limits how fast senders may inject traffic. Used carefully together, they can emulate circuit switching or give delays that are bounded with high probability. Disabling flow control would increase congestion, and IP addresses identify endpoints rather than reserving capacity. Statistically bounded delay is still not a hard worst-case bound.

questions.question: A wire between two telephone switches can carry up to 10,000 simultaneous calls, and each call is given its own fixed slot. What trade-off does that static allocation make?

options.text: Predictable bandwidth per call, but slots sit idle and wasted when unused
Higher utilization, because idle slots are lent to whichever callers are speaking
Lower cost per byte, because static allocation avoids any queueing overhead
Variable delay, because calls compete for the slots in every frame

questions.explanation: The wire is divided statically: even if yours is the only call and the other 9,999 slots are unused, your circuit still gets exactly the same fixed bandwidth as when the wire is full. That gives predictable bandwidth and no queueing, but capacity that no call is using cannot be used by anyone else, so utilization is low and each byte is more expensive.

questions.question: Why does the internet share network bandwidth dynamically between packets instead of reserving it per connection?

options.text: To maximize utilization of the wire, making each byte cheaper, at the cost of queueing
To guarantee a bounded delay to every flow, by spreading its packets evenly across all available links
To give every sender a fixed equal share whatever its demand
Because dynamic sharing removes the need for switches to queue packets

questions.explanation: On the internet, senders jostle to get their packets over the wire as quickly as possible, and switches decide from one moment to the next which packet to send. Idle capacity is used immediately by whoever has data, which maximizes utilization; since the wire has a fixed cost, better utilization makes each byte cheaper. The downside is queueing and therefore variable, unbounded delay.

questions.question: If an operating system shares each CPU core dynamically between several threads, what latency trade-off results?

options.text: Better utilization, but threads wait variable times in the run queue
Guaranteed time slices for each thread, at the cost of lower utilization
Lower utilization of the cores, but bounded response times for each thread
No effect on latency, because modern schedulers are fully deterministic

questions.explanation: With dynamic CPU sharing, one thread sometimes has to wait in the operating system's run queue while another runs, so a thread can be paused for varying lengths of time. That uses the hardware better than allocating a static number of CPU cycles to each thread, which would give predictable timing but waste unused cycles. The same utilization argument motivates virtual machines, and it mirrors the network case.

questions.question: Which resource policy makes latency guarantees achievable, and at what cost?

options.text: Static partitioning (dedicated hardware and bandwidth), at the cost of lower utilization
Dynamic partitioning, which gives both bounded delay and lower cost
Static partitioning, which also turns out cheaper overall because it avoids queueing and retransmission
Dynamic partitioning with more spare capacity, which makes variable delay disappear at no extra cost

questions.explanation: Latency guarantees are achievable if resources are statically partitioned, but reserved capacity sits idle when unused, so utilization drops and the system costs more. Multi-tenancy with dynamic resource partitioning utilizes hardware better and is cheaper, but its downside is variable delay. Variable delays in networks are therefore not a law of nature but the result of a cost/benefit trade-off.

questions.question: In currently deployed technology (as of the late 2010s), where is network quality of service generally not enabled, so that systems must assume unbounded delays?

options.text: In multi-tenant datacenters, public clouds, and over the internet
Only inside private datacenters that you own outright
Only on wireless networks, where interference dominates
Nowhere: quality of service is enabled by default on modern networks

questions.explanation: Quality of service could in principle give statistically bounded delays, but it is not enabled in multi-tenant datacenters and public clouds, or when communicating over the internet. Deployed technology therefore cannot guarantee network delay or reliability, so software has to assume congestion, queueing and unbounded delays will happen, and timeouts have to be determined experimentally. (Internet service providers can buy dedicated bandwidth at the level of whole networks, but that is not per-connection QoS between hosts.)

questions.question: True or false: an asynchronous network has bounded delay; a synchronous network avoids queueing because bandwidth is reserved at every hop; TCP turns an unbounded-delay network into a bounded-delay one; statistically bounded delay is the same as bounded delay.

options.text: False, true, false, false
True, true, true, true
False, false, true, true
True, false, false, true

questions.explanation: First statement false: an asynchronous network has unbounded delay; it tries to deliver quickly but has no upper limit. Second true: a synchronous (circuit-switched) network reserves bandwidth at every hop, so data does not queue and the maximum latency is fixed. Third false: TCP adds retransmission, deduplication and ordering, but cannot remove delay, and retransmission itself adds delay. Fourth false: statistically bounded delay (for example via QoS and admission control) holds with high probability, whereas bounded delay is a hard worst-case limit.

questions.question: Applications use clocks to answer questions. Which of these questions measure a duration (an elapsed interval) rather than a point in time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Has this request timed out yet?
What is the 99th percentile response time of this service?
How many queries per second did this service handle on average over the last five minutes?
At what date and time should this reminder email be sent?

questions.explanation: Some clock questions measure the interval between two events (a request being sent and its response arriving, the length of a five-minute window), while others name a point in time (a publication date, a scheduled send time, a log timestamp). The distinction matters because durations are best measured with a monotonic clock, while points in time need a time-of-day clock tied to a calendar.

optionExplanations.a: A timeout compares the time elapsed since the request was sent with a limit, which is a duration measurement on one machine.
optionExplanations.b: Each response time is the interval between a request arriving and its response being sent, so percentiles of response time are statistics over durations.
optionExplanations.c: Queries per second over the last five minutes counts events within an elapsed window, which is a rate over a duration.
optionExplanations.d: A reminder's send time is a specific calendar date and time, a point in time that needs a time-of-day clock rather than an elapsed interval.

questions.question: What is the core reason time is tricky in a distributed system?

options.text: Messages take a variable, unknown time to cross the network, so event order is hard to determine
Computer clocks are cheap components, so their values cannot be read with any useful precision by software
Machines in different time zones report different local times
Leap seconds occur at unpredictable times that cannot be announced, so no clock can be set correctly

questions.explanation: Communication is not instantaneous: a message is always received later than it was sent, but because network delays vary, the receiver cannot know how much later. On top of that, each machine has its own imperfect clock. Together these make it hard to determine the order in which things happened across machines. Time zones are a display issue (clocks typically count UTC-based seconds), and leap seconds are announced in advance; both are minor compared with variable delay.

questions.question: What hardware device usually provides a computer's local clock?

options.text: A quartz crystal oscillator
An atomic clock, synchronized by GPS directly
A software counter, synchronized by the operating system
A network timestamp, with no local device

questions.explanation: Each machine's clock is an actual hardware device, usually a quartz crystal oscillator. These are not perfectly accurate: they run slightly fast or slow, and the rate varies with temperature, so each machine has its own notion of time. Atomic clocks and GPS receivers are used as more accurate reference sources (for example by NTP servers), not as the ordinary per-machine clock, and the operating system counts the oscillator's ticks rather than generating time by itself.

questions.question: What does a time-of-day clock return?

options.text: The current date and time by some calendar (wall-clock time), e.g. seconds since the 1970 epoch
The number of nanoseconds since the computer was started
A monotonically increasing counter with no calendar meaning
The number of seconds since the year 2000 by the local calendar, including every leap second that occurred

questions.explanation: A time-of-day clock returns the current date and time according to some calendar, also called wall-clock time. For example, clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) on Linux and System.currentTimeMillis() in Java return seconds (or milliseconds) since the epoch, midnight UTC on January 1, 1970, not counting leap seconds. Because it is synchronized with NTP, a timestamp from one machine ideally means the same as one from another, but it can jump. A counter since boot with no calendar meaning describes a monotonic clock.

questions.question: Which properties of time-of-day clocks make them unsuitable for measuring elapsed time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the clock is too far ahead of the NTP server, it may be reset and jump back in time
They often ignore leap seconds, so the represented timeline is not continuous
An NTP reset can also make them jump suddenly forward, inflating a measured interval
Their values are meaningless across machines, so even subtraction on one machine is invalid

questions.explanation: Measuring elapsed time means subtracting a start reading from an end reading, which only works if the clock moves forward steadily. Time-of-day clocks can be forcibly reset by NTP, jumping backward or forward, and they often ignore leap seconds; these discontinuities make them unsuitable for durations. (They also historically had coarse resolution, such as 10 ms steps on older Windows, though that is less of a problem now.) Their values are meant to be comparable across machines, which is their purpose.

optionExplanations.a: A backward reset makes the end reading smaller than it should be, producing a negative or understated duration for an operation that took positive time.
optionExplanations.b: Ignoring leap seconds means some real seconds are not represented consistently, so subtracting two readings across a leap second can give the wrong interval.
optionExplanations.c: A forward jump, for example when NTP forcibly corrects a lagging clock, adds time that never elapsed to any duration measured across it.
optionExplanations.d: Time-of-day clocks are synchronized precisely so their values are comparable across machines; the problem is jumps, not meaningless values.

questions.question: What property defines a monotonic clock?

options.text: It is guaranteed always to move forward, never jumping backward
It returns calendar time that is guaranteed to match UTC
It is synchronized so that all machines in a cluster agree on its value
It moves backward whenever NTP corrects the machine's time

questions.explanation: A monotonic clock, such as clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) on Linux or System.nanoTime() in Java, is named for the guarantee that it always moves forward, whereas a time-of-day clock may jump back. That makes it suitable for measuring durations such as timeouts and response times. Its absolute value has no calendar meaning, and it is not synchronized across machines.

questions.question: How is a monotonic clock meant to be used?

options.text: Read it twice on one machine and take the difference as elapsed time
Compare its values from different machines to order events between them
Store its absolute value as a timestamp for later reading by other systems
Convert its value into a calendar date and time for log messages

questions.explanation: You check a monotonic clock at one point, do something, and check it again; the difference tells you how much time elapsed. Its absolute value is meaningless, perhaps nanoseconds since the computer started, so it makes no sense to compare values from two different computers, to store them as timestamps, or to convert them to dates.

questions.question: On a server with multiple CPU sockets, what complication affects the monotonic clock?

options.text: Separate timers per CPU socket, which the OS tries to hide
There is one timer shared by all sockets, so no complication arises
The operating system exposes each socket's timer separately
Multi-socket servers cannot provide a monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: Each CPU may have its own timer that is not necessarily synchronized with the others. Operating systems compensate for any discrepancy and try to present a monotonic view of the clock to application threads even as they move between CPUs, but this guarantee of monotonicity should be taken with a pinch of salt. The hardware is not a single shared timer, and applications are not normally exposed to the individual timers.

questions.question: How may NTP adjust a machine's monotonic clock?

options.text: It may slew the clock rate, by up to about 0.05%, but cannot make the value jump
It may step the clock's value backward to match the NTP server
It may jump the value forward, but never slow the clock's rate
It cannot affect the monotonic clock's rate or value in any way

questions.explanation: If NTP detects that the local quartz runs faster or slower than the server, it may adjust the rate at which the monotonic clock advances; this is called slewing. By default the rate can be sped up or slowed down by up to 0.05%, but NTP cannot make the monotonic clock jump forward or backward. 0.05% is 500 parts per million, so slewing can correct about 1.8 seconds per hour (3,600 s x 0.0005) without any discontinuity.

questions.question: Why is a monotonic clock usually fine for measuring timeouts in a distributed system?

options.text: Because measuring elapsed time needs no cross-node synchronization
Because monotonic clocks are synchronized by NTP across nodes
Because their absolute values are comparable between machines
Monotonic clocks are unsuitable here, and time-of-day clocks are preferred

questions.explanation: Measuring a timeout involves only one machine's clock: you note the time when you send a request and compare later readings on the same machine. That needs no synchronization between nodes and is not sensitive to slight rate inaccuracies. Monotonic clocks are not synchronized across nodes and their absolute values are not comparable, which is why they are useless for ordering events between machines but fine for durations.
