questions.question: Which properties belong to the monotonic clock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is meaningless to compare its values across machines
It can be slewed but never jumped by NTP
It is the right tool for measuring a service's response time
It counts seconds since a calendar epoch

questions.explanation: A monotonic clock measures elapsed time on one machine: its values are not comparable across machines, NTP may slew its rate but cannot make it jump, and it is the right tool for measuring a response time. Counting seconds since a calendar epoch is the defining behavior of a time-of-day clock instead.

optionExplanations.a: Each machine chooses its own monotonic origin, often boot-related, so raw values from different machines have no meaningful common reference.
optionExplanations.b: NTP may slightly change a monotonic clock's rate to correct drift, but preserving nondecreasing values keeps duration measurements safe.
optionExplanations.c: Response time is an elapsed interval on one machine, exactly the use case for a clock that cannot move backward.
optionExplanations.d: Seconds since a shared calendar epoch describe a time-of-day clock; monotonic clocks deliberately avoid claiming a real-world date.

questions.question: Google assumes the quartz clocks in its servers may drift by up to 200 ppm (parts per million). How much error does that allow for a clock resynchronized every 30 seconds, and for one resynchronized only once a day?

options.text: About 6 ms per 30 seconds; about 17 seconds per day
About 0.06 ms per 30 seconds; about 0.17 seconds per day
About 60 ms per 30 seconds; about 170 seconds per day
About 0.6 ms per 30 seconds; about 1.7 seconds per day

questions.explanation: 200 ppm means the clock can gain or lose 200 millionths of a second per second, 0.0002 s/s. Over 30 seconds: 30 x 0.0002 = 0.006 s = 6 ms. Over a day: 86,400 x 0.0002 = 17.28 s, about 17 seconds. The other options correspond to 2 ppm, 2,000 ppm and 20 ppm. Drift also varies with temperature, and it limits the best accuracy you can achieve even when everything works correctly.

questions.question: What happens when a computer's clock differs too much from its NTP server?

options.text: It refuses to synchronize, or the local clock is forcibly reset
It slews the clock gradually, with no visible jump at all
It raises an error that is reported to every application
It shuts the machine down to prevent data corruption

questions.explanation: If a machine's clock is too far from the NTP server, the client may refuse to synchronize, or the local clock may be forcibly reset. Applications that read the time before and after such a reset may see time go backward or suddenly jump forward. NTP normally slews small differences gradually, but a large offset is beyond what slewing can handle, and the reset happens silently rather than being reported to applications.

questions.question: What fundamentally limits how accurately NTP can synchronize a clock over the internet?

options.text: Variable network delay: one experiment saw at least about 35 ms of error, with spikes near a second
The resolution of the local clock, which is about one second on most systems
The number of servers queried, since accuracy improves without limit as more are added
Nothing: NTP achieves microsecond accuracy over any network connection

questions.explanation: NTP synchronization can only be as good as the network delay, because the client estimates the server's time from messages whose delays are unknown and variable. One experiment found a minimum error of about 35 ms when synchronizing over the internet, with occasional delay spikes causing errors around a second, and large delays can make the NTP client give up entirely. Clock resolution is far finer than a second on modern systems, and querying more servers helps reject outliers but cannot remove delay uncertainty.

questions.question: Some public NTP servers are wrong or misconfigured, reporting a time that is off by hours. Why are NTP clients nonetheless fairly robust to this, and what risk remains?

options.text: They query several servers and ignore outliers, but you still rely on time told by strangers on the internet
They trust a single configured server, which is safe because NTP servers are never wrong
NTP servers can be off by a few milliseconds at most, so no protection is needed
Clients ignore all servers and keep the local clock, so wrong servers have no effect

questions.explanation: NTP clients query several servers and discard those whose times are outliers, so a single server that is hours wrong is usually ignored. Even so, it is somewhat worrying to bet the correctness of your systems on time reported by an unknown party on the internet: if enough servers are wrong, or the client is misconfigured, the error passes through. Ignoring all servers would leave the local clock drifting unchecked.

questions.question: How do virtual machines affect the clock that an application sees?

options.text: The clock is virtualized; while another VM uses the core, the guest pauses and its clock jumps forward
The hypervisor guarantees each VM a perfectly accurate clock, so timekeeping inside a VM is easier than on hardware
The guest's clock runs backward after a pause to compensate for the lost time
VM clocks are unaffected, because each guest reads the host's quartz oscillator directly and never pauses

questions.explanation: In a virtual machine the hardware clock is virtualized, which makes accurate timekeeping harder. When a CPU core is shared between virtual machines, each VM is paused for tens of milliseconds while another runs; from the application's point of view, the clock suddenly jumps forward. This is the same pausing that makes the hypervisor buffer incoming network data and increases network delay variability.

questions.question: If your software runs on devices you don't fully control, such as mobile or embedded devices, how far can you trust the device's hardware clock?

options.text: Hardly at all: users may deliberately set it wildly wrong, e.g. to get around time limits in games
Fully, because mobile carriers and device vendors synchronize every device's hardware clock precisely
Fully, because embedded and mobile devices now ship with GPS-disciplined clocks that users cannot adjust
Mostly, because users have no way to change a device's hardware clock

questions.explanation: On devices outside your control, the hardware clock probably cannot be trusted at all. Some users deliberately set their clocks to incorrect dates and times, for example to circumvent timing limitations in games, so the clock may be set wildly in the past or future. Software that needs trustworthy time should take it from a server it controls rather than from the client device.

questions.question: Under the draft MiFID II European regulation (as of the late 2010s), how closely must high-frequency trading funds synchronize their clocks to UTC, and why?

options.text: Within 100 microseconds, to debug market anomalies and detect manipulation
Within 100 milliseconds, to help produce accurate monthly billing records
Within 1 second, so audit logs can be sorted by the minute and second
Within 1 nanosecond, so that every order is matched in exact sequence

questions.explanation: The draft MiFID II regulation requires high-frequency trading funds to synchronize their clocks to within 100 microseconds of UTC, in order to help debug market anomalies such as flash crashes and to help detect market manipulation. That is far tighter than ordinary NTP over the internet, where errors of tens of milliseconds are typical, and it shows that very good clock accuracy is possible if you invest enough in it.

questions.question: How can an organization such as a trading firm achieve clock accuracy on the order of 100 microseconds?

options.text: GPS receivers, the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), and careful deployment and monitoring
NTP over the public internet, provided enough independent public servers are configured on each machine
Increasing the resolution of each machine's clock so that it reports time in nanoseconds
Disabling NTP and relying on each machine's own quartz oscillator

questions.explanation: Very high accuracy can be achieved with GPS receivers, the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), and careful deployment and monitoring, but it takes significant effort and expertise, and there are many ways it can go wrong: if an NTP daemon is misconfigured or a firewall blocks time traffic, drift quickly produces a large error. Public-internet NTP is limited to tens of milliseconds by network delay, finer resolution does not improve accuracy, and an unsynchronized quartz clock drifts.

questions.question: True or false: a drifting clock usually announces itself by failing loudly; NTP can be more accurate than the network round-trip time; a misconfigured NTP server reporting a time off by hours will typically be ignored by clients; clock drift is a constant per machine.

options.text: False, false, true, false
True, true, true, true
False, true, false, true
True, false, true, false

questions.explanation: First false: a drifting clock usually fails silently; most things keep working while its time moves further from reality. Second false: NTP's accuracy is limited by network round-trip time, because it estimates offsets from messages with unknown delays. Third true: NTP clients query several servers and ignore outliers, so a single server that is hours wrong is typically excluded. Fourth false: drift varies, for example with the machine's temperature.

questions.question: Why are broken clocks worse than broken CPUs?

options.text: A bad clock corrupts data silently instead of stopping the node
A broken clock crashes the machine, whereas a broken CPU does not
A broken clock is always caught immediately by monitoring
The two kinds of fault are equally noticeable in practice

questions.explanation: A clock can drift far from UTC while its process continues serving requests normally. Because the failure is silent, systems need independent offset monitoring.

questions.question: If your software requires synchronized clocks, what is essential to do?

options.text: Monitor clock offsets on all machines and remove nodes that drift too far
Use only time-of-day clocks, never monotonic clocks, for every timing decision
Resynchronize clocks only after an application reports an error caused by time
Nothing further: monitoring is unnecessary once NTP is configured on every machine

questions.explanation: Incorrect clocks easily go unnoticed: a machine whose NTP client is misconfigured keeps working while its clock drifts further from reality, and software relying on synchronized clocks is more likely to lose data silently than to crash. So you must carefully monitor the clock offsets between all machines and declare dead, and remove from the cluster, any node whose clock drifts too far, noticing broken clocks before they cause too much damage. Waiting for application errors is too late, because the damage is silent.

questions.question: In a multi-leader database, client A writes x = 1 on node 1; the write replicates to node 3; client B then increments x to 2 on node 3; both writes replicate to node 2. Each write is tagged with the originating node's time-of-day clock, and node 2 resolves conflicts by last write wins (LWW). How can B's increment be lost?

options.text: If node 3's clock is slightly behind node 1's, x = 2 gets an earlier timestamp and is discarded
LWW always discards whichever write arrives at node 2 second, regardless of the timestamps attached to them
Node 2 detects the conflicting writes and discards both of them
Only if node 3's clock is ahead of node 1's, since a later timestamp on x = 2 is what makes LWW discard it

questions.explanation: B's increment is causally later than A's write, since B saw x = 1 and incremented it. But LWW keeps the value with the greatest timestamp, and the timestamps come from two different nodes' clocks. If node 3's clock lags node 1's even by a few milliseconds, x = 2 can be stamped earlier than x = 1, so node 2 concludes x = 1 is more recent and silently drops x = 2. LWW mistakes timestamp order for causal order; a node 3 clock that is ahead would actually order them correctly.

questions.question: Two nodes' time-of-day clocks are synchronized to within 3 ms. A write on one node is followed, causally, by a write on the other node 1 ms later. Can last-write-wins timestamps order these writes incorrectly?

options.text: Yes: with up to 3 ms of skew, the later write can receive an earlier timestamp
No: 3 ms of skew is small enough to order writes made 1 ms apart
No: causally related writes take their timestamps from one node's clock
Only if one of the clocks is ignoring leap seconds at that moment

questions.explanation: To order two events correctly by timestamp, the clocks must be more accurate than the time between the events. Here the writes are 1 ms apart but the clocks may differ by up to 3 ms, so the second node's clock can read earlier than the first's and the causally later write gets a smaller timestamp. Synchronization to within 3 ms is probably better than you can expect in practice, and it still is not enough.

questions.question: A database uses last write wins. Node 2 receives x = 1 with timestamp 42.004 s and x = 2 with timestamp 42.003 s, although x = 2 was written causally after x = 1 (it incremented it). What does node 2 do?

options.text: Keeps x = 1 and silently discards x = 2
Detects the causality violation and reports an error to the client
Keeps both values as siblings for the application to merge later
Keeps x = 2, because it was the later write to reach node 2

questions.explanation: Last write wins orders writes only by their attached timestamps. Since 42.004 is greater than 42.003, node 2 concludes x = 1 is the more recent value and drops x = 2, so client B's increment is lost with no error reported. Keeping siblings requires causality tracking such as version vectors, which LWW does not do, and arrival order is not what LWW uses. Generating timestamps on clients instead of servers does not fix the underlying problem.

questions.question: What is wrong with last write wins (LWW) as a conflict-resolution strategy based on time-of-day timestamps? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A lagging clock can make many valid writes silently disappear
Timestamps cannot distinguish causal order from concurrency
Equal timestamps need an arbitrary tiebreaker that may violate causality
Last-write-wins causes corruption of the data as it sits on disk

questions.explanation: LWW keeps the value with the greatest timestamp and discards the rest. That has three problems: a node with a lagging clock cannot overwrite values written by a node with a fast clock until the skew has elapsed, so writes silently disappear; timestamps cannot tell writes that happened in quick succession from truly concurrent ones, so version vectors or similar are needed; and two writes can get the same timestamp, especially at millisecond resolution, requiring an arbitrary tiebreaker that can also violate causality. It discards logical versions, but does not corrupt bytes on disk.

optionExplanations.a: A slow clock can timestamp a long sequence below an earlier fast-clock value, causing LWW to discard every one without reporting failure.
optionExplanations.b: Physical timestamps alone do not record whether one operation observed another, so LWW can order a causal update as if it were an independent concurrent write.
optionExplanations.c: Finite clock resolution lets separate nodes produce identical timestamps; an arbitrary secondary ordering resolves the tie but does not preserve causality.
optionExplanations.d: LWW discards logically valid versions according to metadata, but it does not imply byte-level corruption of the values stored on disk.

questions.question: Even with tightly NTP-synchronized clocks, what anomaly can residual clock skew produce in message timestamps?

options.text: A packet sent at 100 ms by the sender's clock arrives at 99 ms by the receiver's clock
A packet arriving 100 ms after it was sent, according to both clocks
The two nodes' monotonic clocks drifting apart, so that local timeouts on each node stop working correctly
Both nodes' clocks jumping backward at exactly the same moment

questions.explanation: Clocks are never perfectly synchronized, so if the sender's clock is slightly ahead of the receiver's and the network is fast, a packet stamped 100 ms by the sender can arrive at 99 ms by the receiver's clock, appearing to arrive before it was sent, which is impossible. A 100 ms delay is ordinary network behavior, and monotonic clocks measure local durations without needing synchronization. The anomaly shows that 'recent' as judged by local clocks may simply be wrong.

questions.question: Could NTP be made accurate enough that incorrect orderings cannot occur?

options.text: Probably not: NTP accuracy is itself limited by the network round-trip time
Yes, by querying more NTP servers at once so their delay errors cancel out
Yes, if local-network NTP usually reports sub-millisecond error
Yes, once quartz drift is removed by resynchronizing frequently

questions.explanation: For correct ordering, the clock source would need to be significantly more accurate than the thing being measured, namely network delay. But NTP's accuracy is itself limited by network round-trip time, as well as by quartz drift. Querying more servers helps reject outliers but cannot cancel the unknown, often asymmetric delay on each exchange; good typical accuracy on a local network is not a guarantee for every pair of closely spaced events; and frequent resynchronization is only as good as each synchronization exchange.

questions.question: What are logical clocks, and how do they differ from physical clocks?

options.text: Incrementing counters that capture only the relative order of events, not elapsed time
Clocks that measure elapsed time more precisely than a quartz oscillator can, using CPU cycle counts
Time-of-day clocks synchronized by NTP to a single logical master server
Monotonic clocks whose absolute values are comparable across machines

questions.explanation: Logical clocks are based on incrementing counters rather than an oscillating quartz crystal. They do not measure the time of day or the number of seconds elapsed, only the relative ordering of events (whether one happened before another), which makes them a safer way to order events across nodes than timestamps. Time-of-day and monotonic clocks, which measure actual time, are called physical clocks.

questions.question: What is the difference between a clock's resolution and its accuracy?

options.text: Resolution is the granularity of readings; accuracy is how close a reading is to true time
They are the same thing on modern hardware, which reports exact time
Accuracy is always finer than resolution on synchronized machines
Resolution is the clock's drift rate per second; accuracy is the size of the smallest step it can report

questions.explanation: You may be able to read a time-of-day clock with microsecond or even nanosecond resolution, but that does not mean the value is accurate to that precision. Quartz drift can easily cause several milliseconds of error even with an NTP server on the local network, and public-internet NTP is probably only accurate to tens of milliseconds, spiking above 100 ms under congestion. If you only know the time to within 100 ms, the microsecond digits are meaningless.

questions.question: A clock reading is best seen as a range with a confidence interval. How can the uncertainty bound be calculated? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Use the attached GPS or atomic clock's stated error range
Combine local drift, server uncertainty and network round-trip time
It is exactly equal to the resolution the clock reports to callers
It is always zero on any clock that is synchronized using NTP

questions.explanation: The uncertainty depends on the time source. A GPS receiver or atomic clock attached directly to the computer has an expected error range reported by its manufacturer. A clock synchronized from a server accumulates expected quartz drift since the last sync, plus the server's own uncertainty, plus the network round-trip time to the server. Most APIs, such as clock_gettime(), do not report this uncertainty, and resolution says nothing about it.

optionExplanations.a: Directly attached precision hardware comes with a manufacturer-specified error range that can form the base of the clock's uncertainty interval.
optionExplanations.b: A network-synchronized clock must allow for oscillator drift since synchronization, the server's uncertainty and uncertainty introduced by the request's network delay.
optionExplanations.c: Resolution says how finely values are represented, not how close they are to UTC; a nanosecond-granularity clock can still be milliseconds wrong.
optionExplanations.d: NTP estimates and reduces error but cannot eliminate variable one-way delay or oscillator drift, so synchronized clocks never have universally zero uncertainty.

questions.question: What does Google's TrueTime API in Spanner return when asked for the current time?

options.text: An interval [earliest, latest] that the true current time is known to lie within
A single exact timestamp guaranteed correct to the nanosecond
A logical counter value that orders events but says nothing about physical time
The measured network round-trip time to the nearest time server

questions.explanation: TrueTime explicitly reports the confidence interval on the local clock: you get back the earliest and latest possible timestamps, and based on its uncertainty calculations the actual current time lies somewhere in between. The width depends on how long it has been since the local quartz clock was last synchronized with a more accurate source. Making uncertainty explicit means non-overlapping intervals prove an order, while overlapping ones honestly say the order is unknown.

questions.question: Snapshot isolation needs monotonically increasing transaction IDs. Why are such IDs hard to generate in a database distributed across many machines and datacenters? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Global monotonic IDs require cross-partition coordination
IDs must order a reader after the transaction it observed
A central ID generator becomes a high-rate bottleneck
Each ID must be a globally unique string rather than a number

questions.explanation: On one node a simple counter suffices, but across partitions a global, monotonically increasing ID requires coordination. The ID must also reflect causality: if transaction B reads a value written by A, B needs a higher ID than A, or the snapshot would be inconsistent. With many small, rapid transactions, a central generator becomes an untenable bottleneck. Distributed generators such as Twitter's Snowflake hand out blocks of IDs to nodes and scale well, but they cannot guarantee ordering consistent with causality. The format of the ID (string or number) is irrelevant.

optionExplanations.a: One strictly increasing sequence across partitions needs nodes to coordinate ownership of the next number, adding latency and a shared serialization point.
optionExplanations.b: Snapshot visibility needs a reader transaction's ID to follow the transaction whose write it observed; uniqueness alone does not encode that causal relationship.
optionExplanations.c: Routing every small transaction through one sequence service can exhaust its throughput and make it a system-wide availability dependency.
optionExplanations.d: Transaction IDs need suitable uniqueness and ordering semantics, but they are not required to be string values; numeric and structured identifiers are common.

questions.question: Spanner uses TrueTime confidence intervals as transaction timestamps for snapshot isolation across datacenters. What observation about two intervals A and B makes this work?

options.text: If the intervals do not overlap, the one that ends first definitely happened earlier
If the midpoints of the intervals differ, the earlier midpoint happened first
If the intervals overlap, the order is determined by comparing node IDs
Comparing two intervals can never establish which event happened first

questions.explanation: Each interval contains the true time of its event. If A's latest possible time is earlier than B's earliest possible time, the intervals do not overlap and B definitely happened after A; there can be no doubt. Only when the intervals overlap is the order uncertain. Midpoints can mislead because the true time could be anywhere in each interval, and node IDs break ties arbitrarily without reflecting real order.

questions.question: Why does Spanner deliberately wait for the length of the TrueTime confidence interval before committing a read-write transaction?

options.text: So any transaction that later reads the data has a non-overlapping interval
To give NTP time to resynchronize the local clock before the commit
To let replicas in other datacenters acknowledge the write before the commit becomes visible to readers
To batch several transactions together for higher commit throughput

questions.explanation: Waiting out the uncertainty interval ensures that any transaction that may read the committed data starts at a sufficiently later time, so the two confidence intervals cannot overlap and the timestamp order reflects causality. To keep this wait short, Google (at the time of writing) deployed a GPS receiver or atomic clock in each datacenter, synchronizing clocks to within about 7 ms. Replication acknowledgment and batching are separate concerns; the wait exists purely because of clock uncertainty.

questions.question: In a database with a single leader per partition, how does a time-limited lease let another node take over if the leader fails?

options.text: The leader renews the lease before expiry; if it stops renewing, another node takes over at expiry
Leadership lasts until the leader resigns voluntarily, so failover always needs an operator to step in
Every node holds its own lease, so several leaders can safely coexist and each accepts writes for the partition
The lease never expires while the leader's process is still running

questions.explanation: A lease is like a lock with a timeout: only one node can hold it at a time, so its holder knows it is the leader until the lease expires. To remain leader it must periodically renew the lease. If the node fails, it stops renewing, so once the lease expires another node can obtain it and take over without anyone needing to confirm that the old leader is dead.

questions.question: A leader's request loop checks that its lease has at least 10 seconds remaining (renewing it if not), then processes the request. Even if it uses only the local monotonic clock, why is this unsafe?

options.text: The thread may pause, e.g. for GC, for over 10 s after the check and then act on an expired lease
It renews the lease far too often, wasting network bandwidth and overloading the lock service with requests
A monotonic clock is unable to measure how long a lease has left, so the remaining-time check is meaningless
It is safe as long as NTP is running correctly on every machine, because the clocks then agree closely enough

questions.explanation: The code assumes very little time passes between checking the lease and processing the request. If the thread is paused for, say, 15 seconds just after the check, the lease will likely have expired and another node may already be leader, yet when the thread resumes nothing tells it that it was paused, so it processes the request unsafely. (Comparing a lease expiry set by another machine against the local time-of-day clock is a second problem, which a monotonic clock fixes; the pause problem remains.)

questions.question: Can a 'concurrent' garbage collector, such as the HotSpot JVM's CMS, eliminate stop-the-world pauses?

options.text: No: it reduces them, but even concurrent collectors must stop the world at times
Yes: concurrent collectors run fully in parallel with the application code
Yes, provided the garbage collector's settings are tuned carefully enough
Yes, because concurrent collection keeps every pause below a few milliseconds in practice

questions.explanation: Many language runtimes need to stop all running threads occasionally for garbage collection, and such stop-the-world pauses have sometimes lasted several minutes. Concurrent collectors cannot fully run in parallel with application code; they still stop the world now and then. Changing allocation patterns or tuning GC settings can often reduce pauses, but robust guarantees must assume the worst.

questions.question: Which causes suspend an entire machine, not just one thread? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Suspending and later resuming an entire virtual machine
Live-migrating a virtual machine between physical hosts
Suspending a laptop when its user closes the lid
Network interface resets, which suspend the CPU for their duration

questions.explanation: VM suspension, live migration and laptop sleep pause every process on the machine. The software cannot renew leases or observe elapsed work while stopped, so peers may legitimately move on.

optionExplanations.a: Suspending a virtual machine freezes all of its processes and memory image until resume, so every application thread stops together.
optionExplanations.b: Live migration may briefly stop the entire guest while final memory changes transfer and execution switches to the destination host.
optionExplanations.c: Laptop sleep halts the operating system and all processes until the user resumes the device, potentially after an arbitrary wall-clock interval.
optionExplanations.d: A network-interface reset interrupts communication but does not normally suspend the machine's CPU or every process for the reset duration.

questions.question: In a virtual machine, what is steal time?

options.text: CPU time spent running other VMs while this one waits
CPU time consumed by the garbage collector inside the guest
Time lost to clock drift between the nodes of a cluster
Time the guest loses when NTP slews its clock rate

questions.explanation: When the hypervisor switches to a different virtual machine, the currently running thread in this VM is paused at an arbitrary point in its code, and the CPU time spent in other VMs is called steal time. If the machine is under heavy load with a long queue of threads waiting to run, it may take a while before the paused thread runs again. To the application, this is just another unannounced pause.

questions.question: How can synchronous disk I/O pause a thread even if the code never explicitly accesses a file?

options.text: Runtimes can touch disk implicitly, such as Java lazily loading class files on first use
It cannot: only code that explicitly opens files ever blocks on disk I/O
Disk pauses are bounded by seek time, so they never last more than a few milliseconds
Network block storage such as Amazon EBS removes I/O pauses entirely

questions.explanation: A thread performing synchronous disk access waits for the I/O to finish, and in many languages disk access happens surprisingly: the Java classloader lazily loads class files when first used, which could be at any point in execution. I/O pauses and GC pauses can even combine. If the 'disk' is a network filesystem or network block device such as EBS, I/O latency also inherits the variability of network delays, so pauses are not bounded by seek time.

questions.question: What is thrashing in a system that allows swapping memory pages to disk?

options.text: The OS spends most of its time swapping pages in and out, doing little work
The garbage collector running so often that the application cannot make progress
Threads being context-switched so frequently that caches are constantly flushed
Repeated CPU cache misses slowing arithmetic down to the speed of memory

questions.explanation: With swapping enabled, a simple memory access may cause a page fault that loads a page from disk, pausing the thread during slow I/O; under high memory pressure that may require evicting another page to disk. In extreme cases the OS spends most of its time moving pages in and out and gets little real work done: thrashing. To avoid it, paging is often disabled on server machines, preferring to kill a process to free memory rather than risk thrashing.

questions.question: Which Unix signal stops a process from getting any CPU time until it is resumed with SIGCONT, and how might it be sent by accident?

options.text: SIGSTOP, e.g. sent by mistake by an operations engineer
SIGKILL, for example by an operator restarting a service
SIGTERM, for example by pressing Ctrl-C in a shell
SIGHUP, for example when an SSH session disconnects

questions.explanation: SIGSTOP immediately stops a process from getting CPU cycles until SIGCONT resumes it, at which point it continues where it left off, unaware it was stopped. Even in environments that never use it deliberately, an operations engineer might send it by accident. (Pressing Ctrl-Z in a shell sends the closely related SIGTSTP, which by default also stops the process.) SIGKILL ends a process outright, SIGTERM asks it to terminate (Ctrl-C sends SIGINT), and SIGHUP typically signals a hang-up or a request to reload; none of them pause and later resume it.

questions.question: Why don't single-machine thread-safety tools such as mutexes, semaphores and atomic counters translate directly to distributed systems?

options.text: Distributed nodes share no memory, only messages sent over an unreliable network
Because mutexes work only on machines whose clocks are monotonic
Because the nodes of a distributed system are typically written in different programming languages
They do translate: a distributed lock behaves exactly like a local mutex

questions.explanation: On one machine, threads coordinate through shared memory, and mutexes and atomic operations rely on it. A distributed system has no shared memory, only messages sent over an unreliable network, and any node can be paused for a long time without noticing while others decide it is dead. That is why a distributed lock needs mechanisms such as leases and fencing tokens rather than behaving like a local mutex.

questions.question: What is a hard real-time system?

options.text: Software that must meet a specified response deadline in all circumstances
Software that pushes data to web clients as soon as it changes
Software optimized to achieve the highest possible throughput
Software with low average latency, but no worst-case timing bound under heavy load

questions.explanation: In hard real-time systems, such as those controlling aircraft, rockets, robots or a car's airbag, there is a specified deadline by which the software must respond, and missing it may cause failure of the entire system. In embedded systems 'real-time' means designed and tested to meet timing guarantees in all circumstances, unlike the vaguer web usage of servers pushing data to clients. Real-time is not the same as high-performance: such systems may have lower throughput because they prioritize timely responses.

questions.question: What does providing real-time guarantees require, and what does it cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A real-time stack with bounded operations and extensive measurement
Restricted language, library and tool choices
High development cost and possibly lower throughput
For server-side data processing real-time guarantees are both economical and by now standard industry practice

questions.explanation: Hard deadlines require a real-time operating system, bounded library operations, controlled allocation and extensive worst-case testing. Those restrictions are expensive and may reduce throughput, so ordinary server systems accept pauses.

optionExplanations.a: Every software layer must document and honor worst-case timing, and measurement must verify the complete system rather than only average performance.
optionExplanations.b: Most languages and libraries permit unbounded pauses from allocation, garbage collection or blocking calls, so hard deadlines sharply narrow the usable ecosystem.
optionExplanations.c: Worst-case engineering, certification and reserved resources are expensive, and prioritizing deadlines may deliberately sacrifice aggregate throughput.
optionExplanations.d: General server-side processing normally favors utilization and flexible tooling; full hard real-time guarantees are too costly to be standard or universally economical.

questions.question: How can a service reduce the user-visible impact of garbage collection pauses?

options.text: Drain traffic or proactively restart one process at a time
Disable garbage collection entirely on the server nodes
Run a real-time operating system for all server workloads
Increase the heap size until garbage collection never runs

questions.explanation: Allocation rate and free-memory trends can warn that collection is approaching. The service can drain a node before GC or roll processes before expensive old-generation collection, hiding many pauses from clients while retaining redundancy.

questions.question: Why can one distributed node not know another node's exact state?

options.text: It learns of others only via messages, and silence cannot distinguish death, delay or pause
Nodes share memory but not clocks, so the only uncertainty is about when other nodes' events happened
Nodes can inspect each other's state directly, so uncertainty is avoidable
Remote nodes deliberately hide their state from other nodes for security

questions.explanation: A node observes other machines only through delayed or missing messages and fallible clocks. It cannot distinguish a crash from a long pause or partition with certainty, so protocols must base decisions on evidence from multiple nodes and preserve causality despite incomplete knowledge.

questions.question: How do you reason about an unreliable system without having to resolve every philosophical question?

options.text: State the assumptions as a system model and design to meet them
Assume the network is reliable and test very thoroughly
Restrict yourself to single-node systems throughout
Accept that reliable behaviour is simply unachievable

questions.explanation: A system model states the delays and fault behaviors an algorithm may encounter. Designers can then prove safety and liveness within those assumptions and test whether the deployment plausibly satisfies them.

questions.question: Which one-sided network fault lets a node still believe it is healthy while the rest of the cluster declares it dead?

options.text: A node that receives every message but whose outgoing messages are dropped
A node whose incoming messages are dropped while its replies get through
A node whose clock is set far in the past, so its messages look stale
A node that lies in its heartbeat replies about its own health

questions.explanation: With an asymmetric fault, the node receives every request and is working perfectly well, but its responses are dropped, so after a timeout the others declare it dead. The node may not even realize anything is wrong, and if it does notice its messages are not acknowledged, it still cannot do anything about it. The moral is that a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment of the situation, so distributed systems rely on a quorum of nodes rather than one node's view. A node that lies is a Byzantine fault, not a network fault.

questions.question: Which situations require that there be only one of some thing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Only one node is allowed to be the leader for a database partition, to avoid split brain
Only one transaction or client is allowed to hold the lock for a particular resource or object, to prevent concurrently writing to it and corrupting it
Only one user is allowed to register a particular username, because a username must uniquely identify a user
Only one node in the whole cluster is permitted to hold a clock reading

questions.explanation: Leadership of a partition (to avoid split brain), ownership of a lock (to prevent corrupting concurrent writes) and ownership of a username (to keep it unique) all require that exactly one party holds a role. The danger in a distributed system is that a node may believe it is the chosen one even though a quorum of nodes has declared it dead and handed the role to someone else, for example after a network interruption or GC pause. Every node has its own clock, so clock readings are not an exclusive resource.

optionExplanations.a: Two simultaneous partition leaders can accept incompatible writes, so election and fencing must ensure that only the current leader's actions take effect.
optionExplanations.b: Mutual exclusion protects a resource by permitting only one valid lock holder at a time, while fencing handles a holder that resumes after losing the lock.
optionExplanations.c: A username is an application uniqueness invariant: accepting two owners for the same identifier would make authentication and references ambiguous.
optionExplanations.d: Every node necessarily has a local clock reading, and distributed algorithms do not require one globally exclusive clock holder; they manage clock uncertainty instead.

questions.question: A storage service lets a client write a file only while it holds a lease from a lock service. How can a client that pauses for a long time corrupt the file anyway?

options.text: Its lease expires mid-pause, another client gets a lease and writes, then the paused one writes too
Its lease is revoked, after which the storage service automatically rejects all of its writes on its own
The lock service grants two leases for the same file at the same moment whenever its holder pauses for long
The storage service's clock jumps backward, which reorders the clients' writes

questions.explanation: If the lease holder is paused for too long, its lease expires and another client can obtain a lease and start writing. When the paused client comes back, it believes (incorrectly) that its lease is still valid and also writes, so the writes clash and the file is corrupted. HBase used to have exactly this bug. The storage service does not automatically know the lease has expired unless it checks something such as a fencing token.

questions.question: How does a fencing token stop a stale lease holder?

options.text: Each grant carries a higher number; the resource rejects any lower than seen
The resource rejects writes stamped earlier than its own clock's current time
The resource accepts writes only from the client ID it registered most recently
The resource rejects any write whose checksum fails to match its contents

questions.explanation: The resource remembers the greatest token it has processed. A client may incorrectly believe an expired lease remains valid, but it cannot make progress because its older token proves that a newer owner has already acted.

questions.question: If ZooKeeper is used as the lock service, which of its values can serve as fencing tokens?

options.text: The transaction ID zxid or the node version cversion, both monotonically increasing
The client's session ID, since every ZooKeeper session is given its own unique identifier
The path name of the ephemeral lock node the client created
The ZooKeeper server's wall-clock timestamp of the lock grant

questions.explanation: A fencing token must be a number that increases every time the lock is granted, so the storage service can reject writes carrying an older token. ZooKeeper's zxid and cversion are guaranteed to be monotonically increasing, so they have the required property. Session IDs and paths are unique but not ordered by grant, and wall-clock timestamps can go backward or be skewed between servers.

questions.question: A resource rejects any writer presenting a stale fencing token. Which class of node misbehavior does that protect against?

options.text: A stale but honest node whose lease quietly expired
Any faulty node at all, including one acting maliciously
Only a node whose clock has drifted relative to the others
A node forging a higher token number to push out the holder

questions.explanation: Fencing blocks an honest but stale process that has not learned its lease expired. It does not defend against a malicious client that forges a higher token; that stronger arbitrary behavior belongs to the Byzantine fault model.

questions.question: What is the Two Generals Problem?

options.text: Two generals must agree using messengers who may be lost
Two generals must agree even though one of them is a traitor
Two generals share a radio channel that may be jammed
Two generals must synchronize their clocks before attacking

questions.explanation: Two generals camped at different sites must agree on a battle plan, but can communicate only by messengers who may be delayed or lost, much like packets in a network. Neither can be sure the other received the latest message. There are no traitors in this problem; the difficulty comes entirely from unreliable communication. It is the basis for discussing consensus, and the Byzantine Generals Problem generalizes it by adding traitors.

questions.question: How does the Byzantine Generals Problem differ from the Two Generals Problem?

options.text: n generals must agree while some of them, not known in advance, are traitors
There are exactly three generals, one of whom is known in advance to be the traitor
Messages are guaranteed to arrive, so only the timing of the attack matters
The messengers rather than the generals are the ones who may be traitors

questions.explanation: In the Two Generals Problem the only difficulty is unreliable messengers. In the Byzantine version, there are n generals who need to agree, most of them loyal and sending truthful messages, but some traitors try to deceive and confuse the others with fake or untrue messages while remaining undiscovered. It is not known in advance who the traitors are. This models nodes that may 'lie' rather than merely fail.

questions.question: In distributed systems, what is a Byzantine fault?

options.text: A node 'lying': sending arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses that break the protocol
A node crashing and never coming back to rejoin the system
A network fault that cuts one group of nodes off from the rest
A node responding very slowly because of a long garbage collection pause, then catching up

questions.explanation: Most of the discussion of distributed systems assumes nodes are unreliable but honest: they may be slow, crash, or have outdated state, but if they respond they follow the protocol. A Byzantine fault is when a node may 'lie', sending arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses, for example claiming to have received a message it never did. The name comes from 'Byzantine' in the sense of excessively complicated and devious, from Lamport's Byzantine Generals Problem; it does not imply anything about historical Byzantium.

questions.question: What does it mean for a system to be Byzantine fault-tolerant?

options.text: It keeps operating correctly even if some nodes malfunction, disobey the protocol, or are attacked
It tolerates crashed nodes, but assumes that every node which does respond is following the protocol
It tolerates malicious attackers, but not nodes that malfunction accidentally
It tolerates network partitions by stopping all processing until they heal

questions.explanation: A system is Byzantine fault-tolerant if it continues to operate correctly even if some of the nodes are malfunctioning and not obeying the protocol, or if malicious attackers are interfering with the network. Both halves matter: a node need not be malicious to be Byzantine, since radiation-corrupted memory produces arbitrary behavior too. Tolerating only crashes, while assuming honest responses, is the ordinary non-Byzantine model.

questions.question: Why must flight control systems tolerate Byzantine faults?

options.text: Because radiation can corrupt memory or CPU registers
Because a pilot may deliberately issue a malicious command
Because flight software is written by untrusted outside vendors
Because air traffic control networks are publicly accessible

questions.explanation: In aerospace environments, radiation can corrupt data in a computer's memory or CPU registers, making a node respond to other nodes in arbitrarily unpredictable ways. Because a system failure would be catastrophic (an aircraft crashing, or a rocket colliding with a space station), flight control systems must tolerate such Byzantine faults. The concern is arbitrary misbehavior caused by corrupted hardware, not malicious pilots, untrusted vendors or public networks: 'Byzantine' describes the behavior, not necessarily an intent to deceive.

questions.question: Besides aerospace systems whose memory can be corrupted by radiation, in what kind of system is Byzantine fault tolerance relevant?

options.text: Systems with several participating organizations, such as blockchains, where some may cheat
Single-organization datacenters, where every node is controlled and administered by one operator
Web applications, where browsers are under the control of untrusted end users
Embedded consumer devices, whose clocks users may deliberately set wrong

questions.explanation: When several mutually untrusting organizations participate, some may attempt to cheat or defraud others, so a node cannot simply trust another's messages. Peer-to-peer networks such as Bitcoin and other blockchains can be seen as a way for untrusting parties to agree whether a transaction happened without a central authority. In a single organization's datacenter nodes can usually be trusted, and web applications handle untrusted browsers by making the server the authority rather than by running Byzantine protocols.

questions.question: Why do most server-side data systems assume no Byzantine faults? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Nodes are usually inside one organizational trust boundary, and radiation-induced memory corruption is rare enough not to dominate the fault model
Datacenter hardware makes arbitrary corruption physically impossible
Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols are substantially more complicated and may require hardware support
The deployment and replication cost is impractical for most server-side systems

questions.explanation: The assumption is pragmatic, not absolute: controlled nodes are usually honest, arbitrary hardware corruption is uncommon, and full Byzantine protocols add substantial complexity and replica cost. Security controls still remain necessary.

optionExplanations.a: Servers under one operator are normally authenticated and administered together, while random arbitrary memory corruption is rare enough that crash faults dominate routine design.
optionExplanations.b: Datacenter hardware can suffer memory, CPU, disk and network corruption; non-Byzantine models are an economic assumption, not a claim of physical impossibility.
optionExplanations.c: Byzantine agreement needs more complex protocols and sometimes trusted hardware or cryptography to handle participants that send inconsistent messages.
optionExplanations.d: Tolerating Byzantine faults usually needs substantially more replicas and communication, making the deployment cost unattractive for ordinary server applications.

questions.question: Web applications must expect arbitrary and malicious behavior from clients such as web browsers. How do they normally handle it?

options.text: Make the server the authority and validate all client input
Run a Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocol among the browsers
Trust client messages, since clients run the site's own JavaScript code
Use quorum voting among clients to decide which requests are valid

questions.explanation: Because clients are under end-user control, input validation, sanitization and output escaping are essential, for example to prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Web applications typically do not use Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols for this; they simply make the server the authority on what client behavior is and isn't allowed. Byzantine fault tolerance becomes more relevant in peer-to-peer networks, where there is no such central authority.

questions.question: Why can't a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm save you from your own bugs?

options.text: Because every node runs the same software and has the same bug
Because a software bug is not a Byzantine fault by definition
Because Byzantine algorithms require unanimity among nodes
It can save you, provided that the bug is sufficiently rare

questions.explanation: A software bug could be regarded as a Byzantine fault, but if the same software is deployed to all nodes, every node has the same bug, so a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm cannot save you. Such algorithms typically require more than two-thirds of the nodes to function correctly; with four nodes, at least three must be correct, so at most one may misbehave. Using that against bugs would require four independent implementations and hoping a given bug appears in only one of them.

questions.question: Why can't a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol realistically protect against attackers exploiting security vulnerabilities?

options.text: An attacker who compromises one node can probably compromise all, as they run the same software
Because Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols work only when every single node behaves honestly
Because security attacks are crash faults rather than Byzantine faults
It can: such a protocol fully replaces authentication, encryption and firewalls

questions.explanation: Byzantine fault tolerance assumes only a minority of nodes misbehave. In most systems, though, if an attacker can compromise one node they can probably compromise all of them, because they are probably running the same software, which breaks that assumption. Traditional mechanisms such as authentication, access control, encryption and firewalls therefore remain the main protection against attackers.

questions.question: What can basic validation and checksums defend against?

options.text: Corruption, bugs and misconfiguration, not attackers
Every Byzantine fault, giving full fault tolerance at low cost
Determined adversaries who deliberately forge their messages
Only network-level faults, which TCP checksums already catch anyway

questions.explanation: These checks cheaply reject accidental nonsense and isolated misconfiguration. An attacker can deliberately forge internally consistent values, so full Byzantine tolerance would require stronger identities, quorums, and independent implementations.

questions.question: Network packets are sometimes corrupted by hardware or software bugs. Why add a checksum in the application-level protocol, above TCP and UDP?

options.text: TCP and UDP checksums usually catch corrupted packets, but sometimes corruption evades them
Because TCP and UDP do not include any checksums at all, leaving corruption entirely undetected
Because an application-level checksum makes data transfer faster than relying on TCP's own checks
To defend against a determined attacker who forges packets with carefully chosen contents

questions.explanation: Packets do sometimes get corrupted by hardware issues or bugs in operating systems, drivers or routers. The checksums built into TCP and UDP usually catch this, but sometimes corruption evades detection. A simple application-level checksum is usually sufficient protection. It guards against accidental corruption, a weak form of 'lying', not against a deliberate adversary who could recompute the checksum.

questions.question: An internal service sits behind a firewall rather than being publicly accessible. What input validation is sensible for it?

options.text: Less strict than a public application's, but still basic sanity checks, e.g. in protocol parsing
Skipping validation entirely, because only trusted internal services are able to reach it
Full Byzantine fault tolerance applied to every request it receives from other services
Only TLS encryption, which also guarantees that message contents are valid

questions.explanation: A publicly accessible application must carefully sanitize all user input, for example checking that values are in a reasonable range and limiting string sizes to prevent denial of service through large memory allocations. An internal service behind a firewall may get away with less strict checks, but some basic sanity-checking of values, for example when parsing protocol messages, is still a good idea, because bugs and misconfiguration produce invalid messages even without attackers. TLS protects transport, not correctness.

questions.question: How does an NTP client identify a misconfigured server?

options.text: The client compares several servers' estimates and discards outliers
The client uses only the first responding server
The client averages all servers including outliers
The client trusts the server with the lowest stratum number unconditionally

questions.explanation: No single external time server is fully trustworthy. Agreement among independent estimates makes one server that is hours wrong detectable, provided most configured sources are reasonably correct.

questions.question: What is a distributed-system model?

options.text: An abstraction of the delays and faults an algorithm assumes
A benchmark of a system's performance under a standard load
A diagram of the machines and network links in one deployment
The concrete code that implements a distributed algorithm

questions.explanation: A proof is meaningful only relative to assumptions about delays, pauses, crashes, recovery, and arbitrary behavior. A system model states those assumptions explicitly so an algorithm can be evaluated independently of one deployment.

questions.question: What bounds does the synchronous system model assume?

options.text: Finite bounds on network delay, process pauses and clock error
Zero delay and perfectly synchronized clocks, which is realistic
Unbounded delay, which makes it the realistic choice
A system without any clocks, relying only on message ordering

questions.explanation: An algorithm may tolerate nonzero latency and clock skew if a known maximum exists. Commodity networks and runtimes occasionally exceed any chosen bound, so the model is useful for reasoning but not a faithful worst-case description.

questions.question: What does the partially synchronous model assume?

options.text: Useful bounds usually, but unbounded delays during some faults
Delays that are always large, but nonetheless bounded
Synchronized clocks, even though network delay is unbounded
Conditions that no deployed system has ever actually exhibited in practice

questions.explanation: Partial synchrony means the system behaves like a synchronous one most of the time, with networks and processes well behaved, but sometimes exceeds the bounds on network delay, process pauses and clock drift, and then those can become arbitrarily large. This is a realistic model of many systems. Algorithms designed for it must keep their safety properties even during the periods when timing assumptions are violated.

questions.question: In the asynchronous system model, what is an algorithm not allowed to do?

options.text: Make any timing assumptions at all, or even use a clock, so no timeouts
Send messages to other nodes; under this model it may only receive them
Use persistent storage to remember state across operations
Assume that the other nodes it exchanges messages with are honest

questions.explanation: In the asynchronous model an algorithm may make no timing assumptions; it does not even have a clock, so it cannot use timeouts. Some algorithms can be designed for this model, but it is very restrictive. It still allows sending messages and using storage, and it is a timing model, separate from the node-fault model that decides whether nodes may be dishonest (Byzantine).

questions.question: Match the three timing system models (synchronous, partially synchronous, asynchronous) to their defining assumptions.

options.text: Synchronous: fixed known bounds; partially synchronous: bounds usually hold; asynchronous: no clock at all
Synchronous: no clock at all; partially synchronous: bounds usually hold; asynchronous: fixed known bounds
Synchronous: bounds usually hold; partially synchronous: no clock at all; asynchronous: fixed known bounds
All three: fixed known bounds on delay, differing only in how accurate the clocks are

questions.explanation: The synchronous model assumes bounded network delay, bounded process pauses and bounded clock error, with a known upper bound (not zero delay). The partially synchronous model behaves like that most of the time but sometimes exceeds the bounds arbitrarily, which is realistic for many systems. The asynchronous model allows no timing assumptions and has no clock, so it cannot use timeouts. Only the synchronous model guarantees bounds all the time.

questions.question: What does the crash-stop node failure model assume?

options.text: A node fails only by crashing, and once it stops it never comes back
A node crashes and then always recovers after a known, fixed delay
A node crashes and then recovers with its in-memory state intact
A node may slow down at times, but never stops responding

questions.explanation: In the crash-stop model, the only way a node can fail is by crashing: it may suddenly stop responding at any moment, and thereafter it is gone forever. That simplifies reasoning, because a failed node never reappears with stale state. The crash-recovery model relaxes this by letting nodes restart after an unknown time, keeping stable storage but losing in-memory state.

questions.question: What does the crash-recovery node failure model assume about a node's state?

options.text: Nodes may crash and recover later; stable storage survives, in-memory state is lost
In-memory state survives a crash, while data on disk is lost
Both in-memory state and on-disk data survive a node crash intact
Both kinds of state are lost, but the recovery time is known in advance

questions.explanation: In the crash-recovery model, nodes may crash at any moment and perhaps start responding again after some unknown time. They are assumed to have stable storage (nonvolatile disk) that is preserved across crashes, while in-memory state is lost. Because recovery time is unknown, other nodes cannot simply wait for a restart. Real implementations must also consider that the assumption can fail, for example if a disk is corrupted.

questions.question: What does the Byzantine (arbitrary) node fault model allow nodes to do?

options.text: Absolutely anything, including trying to trick and deceive other nodes
Only act adversarially, since every faulty node is controlled by an attacker
Only crash or slow down, never behave in any other way
Lie about timing information, but never about the data they hold

questions.explanation: In the Byzantine model nodes may do absolutely anything: lie, send contradictory or corrupted messages, or try to trick other nodes. That makes it the most general node model. It does not require faulty nodes to be malicious, since accidental corruption can produce the same arbitrary behavior, and it places no limit on what kind of information a faulty node may misreport.

questions.question: Combining the timing models (synchronous, partially synchronous, asynchronous) with the node models (crash-stop, crash-recovery, Byzantine), which combination is generally the most useful for modeling real systems?

options.text: Partial synchrony with crash-recovery faults
The synchronous model with crash-stop faults
The asynchronous model with Byzantine faults
The synchronous model with Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: Real networks and processes are usually well behaved but occasionally exceed any timing bound, which is partial synchrony; real nodes crash and restart, losing memory but keeping what is on disk, which is crash-recovery. The synchronous model is unrealistic because unbounded delays and pauses do occur, the asynchronous model is very restrictive, and Byzantine faults can usually be assumed away inside one organization's datacenter.
